title: Mavin sells the majority, keeps the mic: Don Jazzy's exit to Universal
standfirst: UMG's majority stake in Mavin Global is the biggest exit in African entertainment history — and a clean test of whether authoring a sound is the same as owning it.
verificationNote: Confirmed via UMG, Billboard, MBW and Music Ally: UMG announced a majority investment in Mavin Global on 26 Feb 2024; founder/CEO Don Jazzy (Michael Collins Ajereh) and COO Tega Oghenejobo continue to run the label; TPG Growth fully exited while Kupanda Capital remains a minority investor and strategic adviser; in Feb 2025 the two founders were given oversight of all UMG's business in Nigeria and Tega was elevated to President & COO. Deal value is REPORTED, not disclosed: Billboard put Mavin's valuation north of $125m with a sale price in the $150–200m range. The competing Hybe bid is reported. We do not treat the price or the Hybe detail as confirmed.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: Build a full-stack Afrobeats label — hit factory, artist academy, exec pipeline — then run a contested auction at the genre's global peak so a bidding war (reportedly Hybe vs UMG) sets the price. The idea was never just to make stars; it was to make an asset that majors would compete to buy.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: The sound and the roster are unambiguously African-authored: Don Jazzy shaped a decade of Afrobeats and built Rema, Ayra Starr and Crayon in Lagos. But majority equity and the go-forward catalogue economics now sit with UMG. The founders captured a landmark cash exit and kept operational control — real value retention — yet the recurring upside on the work migrates offshore. Strong authorship, only partial ownership.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: Two sides of craft, both high. Operationally Mavin is a proven hit machine with unusual roster depth; on the deal itself the founders held rare terms — continued autonomy, retained leadership, and within a year an expanded mandate over UMG Nigeria. Few African sellers exit this cleanly.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: Reported as the largest exit in African entertainment history, it sets the template and the price for the next wave of label sales — and simultaneously entrenches the pattern of the continent's fastest-growing music market being consolidated under the three majors. High stakes in both directions.

context: On 26 February 2024, Universal Music Group announced a majority investment in Mavin Global, the Lagos label founded in 2012 by Michael Collins Ajereh — Don Jazzy — the producer-entrepreneur who has spent a decade shaping the sound now sold globally as Afrobeats. Mavin is the home of Rema, whose 'Calm Down' became the biggest Afrobeats crossover to date, alongside Ayra Starr, Crayon, Ladipoe, Johnny Drille, Magixx, Bayanni, Boy Spyce and Lifesize Teddy. It is, by roster and by reputation, the most valuable independent label the continent has produced.

The financial terms were not disclosed by either party. What is on the record is the shape of the deal: UMG takes the majority; private-equity backer TPG Growth fully exits; Kupanda Capital — which had invested alongside TPG through the Kupanda Holdings joint venture — stays on as a minority investor and strategic adviser; and founder/CEO Don Jazzy and COO Tega Oghenejobo continue to run the company with autonomy over strategy and talent. Billboard, which first reported the auction, valued Mavin north of $125m and put the likely sale price in the $150–200m range. Those figures are reported, not confirmed — but even at the low end this is described across the trade press as the biggest exit in the history of African entertainment.

The auction context matters as much as the price. Mavin was shopped through a formal process, and the reporting is consistent that UMG was not the only suitor: Hybe, the South Korean company behind BTS, made a competing bid, and by some accounts led early before Mavin chose Universal. A label that a decade ago was a Lagos production house had become an asset that two of the most powerful music companies on earth were willing to fight over. That is the real headline underneath the headline — not that Mavin sold, but that the world's majors now price African catalogue as strategic territory worth contesting.

The deal closed under regulatory approval later in 2024, and the direction of travel was confirmed in February 2025: UMG placed all of its Nigerian business under Don Jazzy and Tega Oghenejobo, with Tega elevated to President and COO of Mavin Global. So this is not a founder cashing out and disappearing. It is a founder selling the majority of the equity and, in exchange, being handed a bigger operating perimeter inside the acquirer. That distinction is the whole case.

The corporate history matters because it explains who was actually being paid out. Mavin was not bootstrapped alone: Kupanda Capital came in as a founding-stage backer, and in 2019 Kupanda and TPG formed the Kupanda Holdings joint venture, deploying an eight-figure investment (reported at around $10m) that carried the label through the pandemic when live-performance revenue collapsed. By 2024, after roughly the standard private-equity holding period, TPG was ready to realise its return. In that light the sale is two transactions stacked into one: a financial exit for the institutional investors, and a partial cash-out plus platform upgrade for the founders. Reading it only as 'Don Jazzy sold his label' misses the capital structure underneath — and the capital structure is exactly where ownership questions live.
strategicBet: UMG's bet is simple and well-capitalised: Afrobeats is the clearest evidence yet that the next Latin- or K-pop-scale global genre is African, and owning the continent's best label is cheaper and faster than building one. The market data underwrites it. Afrobeats was streamed more than 13 billion times on Spotify in 2022, up roughly 500% on 2017; sub-Saharan Africa was the fastest-growing recorded-music region on earth that year, at 34.7% year-on-year per the IFPI — the only region to grow more than 30%. Buying Mavin is buying a proven pipeline into that curve, plus Don Jazzy's A&R instincts, plus a roster with existing crossover records.

Mavin's bet is subtler, and it is a bet about timing and terms, not just money. Selling the majority at the top of a bidding war converts a decade of catalogue and reputation into hard capital and a durable partnership with the world's largest distribution machine — the thing an independent African label cannot build for itself: global radio, playlisting relationships, sync, and legal muscle across every territory. Crucially, the founders did not sell control of the day-to-day or their creative process. They sold equity and bought reach. The Hybe rejection is the tell: Mavin optimised not for the highest headline number alone but for the partner that let them keep authoring the work while owning less of it.

There is a value-capture story here that is genuinely better than the norm, and it should be stated plainly. Don Jazzy and his backers realised a large exit — wealth that landed with a Nigerian founder and an Africa-focused investor (Kupanda) rather than being extracted from artists on a bad recoupment deal. The founders kept their jobs, their autonomy and, within a year, gained a country-wide mandate. Measured against the usual major-label pattern — sign the talent, own the masters, pay the artist last — this is a comparatively founder-friendly outcome. The bet is that proximity to UMG's platform grows the whole pie faster than independence could.

The counter-bet — the risk Mavin is accepting — is dilution of exactly the thing that made it valuable. UMG's stated rationale leans on Mavin's autonomy and its A&R professionals precisely because the danger it must manage is homogenisation: the quiet pull of a global machine toward playlist-safe, formula-driven records that travel easily but sound like everywhere. Commentary around the deal flagged this directly — the fear that major-label incentives could sand the specific, Lagos-made texture off the music, and that creative and staffing decisions could drift toward a distant head office. Mavin's protection against that is contractual (retained control) and personal (Don Jazzy's continued presence). Both are real today; neither is permanent. Autonomy clauses are only as durable as the executives who honour them, and executives change.
creativeMove: The creative move that made the exit possible predates the deal by twelve years: Don Jazzy built Mavin as an institution, not a vanity label. Where many African acts are solo careers with a manager attached, Mavin operates a system — an in-house production sound, a repeatable A&R method, and, explicitly, an Artist Academy and executive-leadership programme designed to manufacture the next generation of talent and the next generation of the people who run talent. That institutional design is what a major actually buys. You cannot acquire a vibe; you can acquire a machine that reliably produces vibes. Mavin made itself acquirable by being systematic.

The second move is the packaging of the sale itself. Running a competitive auction through a specialist advisor, surfacing a credible foreign bidder in Hybe, and holding out for terms that preserved leadership and autonomy — this is deal-making craft that African cultural founders have rarely had the leverage or the advice to execute. The outcome (majority sold, control retained, mandate expanded) is not the default; it was engineered. For MonoKromatik the instructive part is that the creativity here is as much financial and structural as it is musical. Don Jazzy authored a sound and then authored an exit.
africanRead: Here is the MonoKromatik read, and it is deliberately two-handed. On authorship, there is no argument: the sound, the songs, the stars and the system are African-made. Don Jazzy did not license someone else's format or supply a foreign platform with raw talent to be finished abroad. He built the value in Lagos. That is the strongest possible position an African cultural business can hold, and it is why the price was what it was. Authorship, in this deal, was the leverage.

But authorship and ownership are not the same thing, and this deal is the cleanest illustration of the gap. After the transaction, the people who authored the Afrobeats canon own a minority of the company that houses it, and the majority — with the compounding catalogue economics that flow from every future stream of every future hit — sits with a company headquartered in the Netherlands and listed in Amsterdam. The founders captured a large one-time exit and ongoing salaries and control; UMG captured the annuity. In the long run, catalogue is the annuity, and the annuity is where music wealth actually accumulates. This is the same structural fact we flagged in the Warner/Africori read: the continent authors the culture and then sells the majority of the machine that monetises it in perpetuity.

The honest complication is that this is not obviously the wrong trade. An independent African label has no realistic path to UMG's global infrastructure, and the majors have historically been the gatekeepers to the exact scale that made 'Calm Down' a Hot 100 record. Refusing every major-label deal on principle would have meant leaving Mavin under-capitalised while the genre's global moment ran without it. The founder-friendly terms — retained control, an expanded UMG Nigeria mandate, a landmark payout to Africa-side owners — are meaningfully better than the extractive template. The critique is not that Mavin sold; it is what the aggregate of such deals does to the continent. If the three or four best African labels are each, one by one, majority-acquired by the three global majors, then Africa becomes the world's fastest-growing music market and simultaneously the market where the least of the ownership stays home.

The unresolved question — the one worth watching — is whether Don Jazzy's expanded seat inside UMG becomes a lever or a leash. Running all of UMG Nigeria could mean an African executive finally allocating a major's capital toward African artists on African terms. Or it could mean the continent's best label-builder spending his best years growing someone else's balance sheet. The deal terms make the optimistic reading plausible; history makes the pessimistic one prudent. MonoKromatik's position is that the ideal was never 'never sell.' It is to sell from a position where you keep enough ownership that the annuity, not just the exit, stays partly African. Mavin got closer to that than almost anyone before it — and still ceded the majority.

lessons.title: Authorship is the leverage; ownership is the prize.
lessons.body: Don Jazzy could command a majority-of-the-machine price precisely because the value was genuinely African-authored, not rented. But leverage at the negotiating table is not the same as owning the annuity afterward. Build so that authorship is undeniable — then fight to keep enough equity that the recurring catalogue income, not just the exit cheque, stays partly yours.

lessons.title: Sell the majority from strength, not from need.
lessons.body: Mavin ran a contested auction at the genre's peak, surfaced a rival bidder, and held terms that kept leadership and autonomy. That is the difference between selling and being bought. African cultural founders should treat the deal structure — control, board rights, catalogue reversions — as creative work as serious as the music.

lessons.title: Institutions get acquired; vibes get signed.
lessons.body: A major can sign an artist, but it pays real money for a system. Mavin's academy, A&R method and exec pipeline are what made it an asset rather than a roster. If you want an exit that respects your value, build the machine, not just the moment.

lessons.title: An operator's seat inside the acquirer is worth more than the headline price.
lessons.body: Getting Don Jazzy and Tega placed over all of UMG Nigeria is the term that could keep this deal African in substance. Cash is spent once; an operating mandate compounds. When you sell, negotiate for the chair, not just the cheque.

title: Ethiopian Airlines: The State-Owned Company That Beat the Extraction Thesis
standfirst: Africa's largest and most profitable carrier is wholly state-owned, continentally integrated, and self-financing — the working counter-model to every argument that scale must mean surrender of ownership.
verificationNote: Financial and operational figures (revenue, passengers, fleet, profit, ownership, Star Alliance date, academy scale, peer losses) are drawn from company statements, Wikipedia, and named press. FY2024/25 profit for the group is not separately disclosed in the sources retrieved; the $1.053bn profit figure is the reported FY2024 (2023/24) number. MonoKromatik's read of causation — why the model works and what threatens it — is interpretation, flagged as such.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: The strategic insight is geographic and structural, not clever: turn Addis Ababa's central-continental position into a hub that connects Africa to the world, and build every adjacent capability — cargo, maintenance, training — in-house rather than renting it. Not novel in aviation, but executed with a coherence almost no peer sustained.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: This is the whole point. The value is African-owned end to end: wholly held by the Ethiopian state via its sovereign fund, self-financing 30% of a $12.5bn airport from internal resources, training its own pilots and technicians, and owning the hub, the cargo arm and the MRO. It scales without renting reach or handing equity to a foreign carrier — the inverse of the extraction pattern.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: Sustained operational discipline over decades: successive Vision plans hit ahead of schedule, 170 aircraft, 161 destinations, 19.1m passengers, and profitability held through the Derg, civil war and COVID (25 passenger jets converted to freighters in weeks) while peers took bailouts.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: A $7.6bn revenue SOE that employs ~17,600 people, trains aviation professionals for the whole continent, and props up ASKY, Malawi and Zambia carriers. It is the standing proof that an African state enterprise can be world-class — with real downside stakes if governance ever slips.

context: Ethiopian Airlines is the exception that the rest of African aviation is measured against. Founded in 1945 and flying since 1946, it is today the continent's largest carrier by passengers, destinations, fleet and revenue — and, more unusually, its most consistently profitable. For the 2024/25 Ethiopian fiscal year it reported $7.6bn in revenue, an 8% year-on-year rise, carrying 19.1 million passengers (15.2m international, 3.9m domestic) and roughly 785,000 tonnes of cargo across a fleet of more than 150 aircraft. In the prior year it posted a $1.053bn profit. Those are not African numbers graded on a curve; they are competitive with mid-sized global carriers.

What makes the story matter to MonoKromatik is not the balance sheet alone but who owns it. Ethiopian Airlines is wholly owned by the Ethiopian state through Ethiopian Investment Holdings, the country's sovereign wealth fund. There is no foreign carrier holding a strategic stake, no private-equity turnaround, no franchised brand licence. The airline that connects Africa to Beijing, São Paulo, Washington and London is African-owned from the hub to the cockpit — and it got there while its peers, structured more conventionally, went to the wall.

The contrast is stark and current. Kenya Airways — part-owned by KLM under a much-praised strategic partnership — has needed repeated government bailouts and saw losses balloon during COVID, tripling to around $333m in 2020. South African Airways has not turned an annual profit since 2011 and was lined up for roughly a $1bn bailout after accumulating around $1.2bn in losses between 2018 and 2022. Nigeria has spent two decades failing to stand up a durable flag carrier. Across the continent, with a small number of exceptions, national airlines lose money. Ethiopian makes it — at scale, in a low-income country, as a state-owned enterprise. That combination is supposed to be impossible, and the conventional wisdom explains it away as luck or subsidy. It is neither.

The airline is also more than a passenger business, and that matters to how it survives. Its footprint spans cargo — Ethiopian runs one of the largest freighter networks on the continent, serving 68 dedicated cargo destinations — alongside aircraft maintenance, a catering arm, ground services, an in-house technology unit and the training academy. Secondary hubs and logistics nodes reach into Liège, Lomé, Lilongwe and Lusaka. Where a single-line passenger carrier is fully exposed to fuel spikes, currency shocks and demand collapse, Ethiopian sits on a diversified stack of aviation businesses that rarely fail all at once. When one leg buckles, another carries. That structural resilience is not an accident of size; it was deliberately built, decade over decade, as the point of the enterprise.
strategicBet: The bet has two halves, and both cut against orthodoxy. The first is geographic: Addis Ababa sits at a natural crossroads, close enough to serve Europe, the Gulf, Asia and the Americas from a single African hub. Ethiopian built its network as a set of feeder nodes across the continent that funnel traffic through Bole, then out to the world — extending reach while spreading commercial risk. It is a hub-and-spoke model, but one where the hub is African soil and the spokes are African cities, so the connecting revenue and the strategic control stay home rather than being captured by a Gulf or European carrier acting as Africa's involuntary transit lounge.

The second half is vertical integration as sovereignty. Rather than buy training, maintenance and cargo capacity from foreign suppliers, Ethiopian built them. The Ethiopian Aviation Academy — Africa's largest — trains pilots, technicians, cabin crew and managers not only for itself but for carriers across the continent, with a stated ambition to scale toward 4,000 students a year. Cargo has at times contributed more than a third of revenue, and when COVID grounded passenger flying, the airline converted 25 passenger jets to freighters within weeks and kept earning while rivals queued for state aid. Each in-house capability is both a revenue stream and an insurance policy against dependency. This is the authorship question answered operationally: own the whole value chain, and no one can extract rent from the parts you don't control.

Star Alliance membership, secured in December 2011 as only the third African carrier to join, completes the design. It plugged Ethiopian into global code-sharing, frequent-flyer reciprocity and premium corporate contracts — access to Western demand — without surrendering ownership or control. It is the crucial distinction: joining a distribution alliance is renting shelf space; selling equity to the carrier on the other end is renting the whole business. Ethiopian did the first and refused the second. Kenya Airways, by contrast, is the cautionary mirror image — deep foreign equity, deep foreign operational entanglement, and a balance sheet that has needed the Kenyan state to catch it more than once.

Underneath both halves is a financing philosophy that competitors could not sustain. Ethiopian funds growth substantially from its own retained earnings and disciplined debt, not from perpetual injections of taxpayer cash. Committing 30% of the projected $12.5bn cost of the new Bishoftu mega-airport from internal resources is a statement of exactly this: the company can put real skin in the game because it has been allowed to keep its own profits and compound them, rather than having them siphoned off as dividends, patronage jobs or below-cost domestic fares mandated from above. Self-financing is what converts profitability into sovereignty — a carrier that pays for its own fleet renewal answers to route economics, not to whoever holds the cheque.
creativeMove: The genuinely distinctive move is governance, and it is the least glamorous part of the story. Ethiopian is a state-owned enterprise that has, for decades, been run with managerial autonomy from the political class. The airline's own institutional history credits early leadership with negotiating operational independence even under a military dictatorship — an 'institutional firewall' that let professional decision-making override patronage pressure. That firewall is the actual product. It is why fleet orders track route economics rather than ministerial vanity, why the airline reinvests instead of being milked for dividends or jobs, and why successive Vision plans (Vision 2010, Vision 2025) were hit ahead of schedule while the flag carriers that couldn't insulate management from politics bled out.

The continental strategy extends the same logic outward. Ethiopian has taken minority stakes to stand up or stabilise other African carriers — ASKY out of Lomé as a West African feeder, plus Malawi Airlines and Zambia Airways — turning potential competitors into a distributed network of partners that feed the Addis hub. It is empire-building, but of a specific kind: African capital and African expertise underwriting African aviation capacity, rather than the continent's skies being carved up by outside carriers. Vision 2035 sets the ambition explicitly — a fleet toward 271 aircraft, 207 destinations, 65 million passengers and $25bn in revenue, financed on the same self-reliant model that put 30% of a $12.5bn new-airport project on the company's own books.

The Aviation Academy is where the philosophy becomes most legible, because it is the least commercially obvious. A carrier chasing quarterly numbers would buy pilot hours and outsource heavy maintenance; training a continent's worth of aviation professionals is a slow, expensive, generational commitment with diffuse payoff. Ethiopian made it anyway — Africa's largest aviation academy, an ICAO regional training centre, feeding its own cockpits and control rooms and those of carriers across the continent, with ambitions to scale toward 4,000 students a year and a second campus at Hawassa. The strategic effect is twofold: it removes a dependency (the airline never has to bid against foreign carriers for scarce African aviation talent) and it makes Ethiopian the gravitational centre of the continent's aviation human capital. Talent trained on your equipment, to your standards, is talent that flows toward you. That is authorship compounding over decades — you do not just capture today's value, you own the pipeline that produces tomorrow's.
africanRead: MonoKromatik's read: Ethiopian Airlines is the single cleanest counter-example to the extraction thesis in African business. The default pattern we decode — again and again — is an African brand or asset that scales only by renting a foreign platform, licensing a foreign name, or selling the equity that carries the upside, so that reach grows while ownership and value-capture flow offshore. Ethiopian scaled to global relevance and kept every layer: the hub, the cargo arm, the maintenance base, the training pipeline, the equity. It proves the trade-off is not a law of nature. You can be continental and world-class without being a tenant.

The honest downside is that the entire model rests on one fragile input: governance autonomy. The airline works because management has been insulated from political extraction — but that insulation is a norm, not a constitutional guarantee, and Ethiopia's domestic politics have been volatile. The gravest historical threat to the airline came not from creditors or partners but from its own political class; if that firewall ever fails — if orders, routes or the balance sheet become instruments of patronage — the same state ownership that is today the source of the achievement becomes the mechanism of its unwinding. State ownership is not the moat. Disciplined, autonomous management of a state asset is the moat, and moats made of norms can be drained.

There is a second caution. Ethiopian's success is hard to franchise. It draws on a specific geography (Addis's crossroads position, its altitude driving the Bishoftu airport plan for unrestricted long-haul), a long institutional memory, and a scale flywheel that took eighty years to spin up. A Nigerian or Congolese state cannot simply copy the org chart. But the transferable lesson is not the model — it is the principle underneath it: build the adjacent capabilities in-house, keep the equity, and defend management from the people who own you. That is authorship, and it is available to anyone willing to hold the line on it.

lessons.title: Own the adjacent layers, not just the core.
lessons.body: Ethiopian's real edge is that cargo, maintenance and training are in-house — each a revenue line and a hedge against dependency. Scale bought from foreign suppliers is scale someone else can price you out of. Build the parts that make you un-extractable.

lessons.title: An alliance is shelf space; equity is the store.
lessons.body: Star Alliance gave Ethiopian global demand without surrendering control. The peers that sold strategic stakes to foreign carriers rented out the business itself. Know which line you are standing on — reach is rentable, ownership is not to be.

lessons.title: The moat is autonomous management, not the ownership label.
lessons.body: State-owned is not the achievement; state-owned and insulated from patronage is. The same structure that made Ethiopian great could unmake it the day management stops being defended from politics. Guard the firewall like it is the product — because it is.

pullQuotes: The airline that connects Africa to the world is African-owned from the hub to the cockpit — and it got there while its peers went to the wall.
State ownership is not the moat. Disciplined, autonomous management of a state asset is the moat, and moats made of norms can be drained.

title: Carry1st: Owning the Rails, Not the Players
standfirst: A Cape Town publisher decided the money in African gaming was not the games — it was the payment and distribution layer underneath them, and it built that layer before the global studios noticed they needed it.
verificationNote: Funding rounds, named investors (a16z, Google, Sony Innovation Fund, Konvoy, Bitkraft, Riot Games), founders, publishing partners (Riot, Supercell, Activision/Call of Duty: Mobile) and Pay1st's stated coverage (120+ payment methods, six markets) are confirmed by TechCrunch, a16z, GlobeNewswire and Carry1st's own pages. Revenue figures are company-reported growth multiples, not audited absolute numbers. We do NOT confirm any acquisition of Paxful.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: The sharp move is refusing the obvious game: instead of betting on a hit title, Carry1st bet that the binding constraint in African gaming is payments and distribution, and built the toll-road under everyone else's traffic. The 'Garena of Africa' template is borrowed, but applying it to a 55-country payments maze that global studios treated as unreachable is genuinely original positioning.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: Carry1st OWNS the rail — Pay1st is its own gateway and it acts as merchant of record, capturing a cut of every transaction rather than renting someone else's checkout. That is real African-authored infrastructure and value capture. The honest discount: the games themselves are licensed global IP (Riot, Supercell, Activision), and the capital stack is overwhelmingly foreign (a16z, Google, Sony, Konvoy, Bitkraft), so the equity upside is shared far beyond the continent.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: Aggregating 120+ local payment methods across six markets and becoming the merchant of record for blue-chip publishers is hard, unglamorous operational work, and Carry1st has landed the logos to prove the pipes carry real volume. Execution risk now sits in scaling the storefront, not proving the concept.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: If Carry1st becomes the default way Africans pay for games, it captures margin on a market projected to exceed 180 million gamers — meaningful continental stakes. But absolute revenue is undisclosed, the market is still nascent, and the outcome depends on global studios continuing to route through it rather than building direct. Promise is high; proof at scale is still pending.

context: Carry1st was founded in 2018 by Cordel Robbin-Coker, Lucy Hoffman and Tinotenda Mundangepfupfu, and is usually described as a South African — Cape Town-headquartered — mobile games publisher. That description is accurate but incomplete, and the incompleteness is the whole story. The company began as a publisher of its own social and trivia titles, the sort of business where success or failure rides on whether a specific game finds an audience. Somewhere along the way its founders concluded that the games were the least defensible part of the opportunity.

The reasoning was demographic and structural. Africa has roughly 1.3 billion people with a median age of about 19, overwhelmingly mobile-first, and — crucially — almost entirely locked out of the global games economy. Not because Africans do not want to play or pay, but because the machinery that collects their money does not exist in a form international studios can use. a16z, which would later lead a round, framed the barrier precisely: the continent runs on more than 270 mobile wallets, 500-plus banks and several card networks spread across 55 countries. Most mobile games, meanwhile, accept only PayPal or international credit cards — instruments with negligible penetration across most of Africa. A teenager in Lagos or Nairobi with airtime and a mobile-money balance simply could not buy a battle pass.

So Carry1st reframed its own business. Publishing games would remain the front door — it is how you learn what players want and how you earn the right to partner with global studios — but the enduring asset would be the layer underneath: a payments and distribution rail purpose-built for African consumers. The company raised progressively larger rounds against that thesis: a $6M Series A in May 2021 (Riot Games, Konvoy Ventures, Raine Ventures, TTV Capital), a $20M extension in January 2022 led by Andreessen Horowitz with Google's Africa Investment Fund, Avenir and the musician Nas participating, and a $27M pre-Series B in January 2023 led by Bitkraft Ventures with a16z and Konvoy returning. In January 2024 Sony Group's Sony Innovation Fund made Carry1st the inaugural investment out of its new Africa-focused fund.

That investor roster — a16z, Google, Sony, Konvoy, Bitkraft, Riot Games — is the tell. These are not African patient-capital funds hoping for modest returns. They are the world's most template-literate gaming and technology backers, and they were pattern-matching Carry1st against Sea Limited's Garena in Southeast Asia: a company that used gaming as the wedge to build payments and commerce, and became a regional consumer-internet giant in the process.
strategicBet: The strategic bet is a deliberate inversion of where most people look for value in gaming. The visible money in games is the games — the hits, the IP, the download-chart glory. Carry1st decided that in Africa specifically, the hits would mostly belong to studios in California, Helsinki and Seoul, and that chasing them was a loser's game for an African company. The durable money was in the rails: the payment collection, foreign-exchange handling, tax and compliance work, and the storefront that sits between a global publisher and an African wallet. Own that, and you earn on every transaction regardless of which game is hot this quarter.

This is why Pay1st matters more than any single title. Pay1st is Carry1st's proprietary payment gateway, offering — by the company's own account — 120-plus local payment methods across six geographies: South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, Morocco and Ghana, mobile money included. Its pitch to a global studio is blunt and attractive: integrate once, and you can accept money from African players without touching compliance, tax, FX or fraud risk yourself. Carry1st becomes the merchant of record, collects locally in dozens of currencies, and settles to the publisher in USD. The publisher gets reach it could not build; Carry1st gets a permanent toll on the flow.

The second half of the bet is that publishing and payments reinforce each other rather than competing for attention. Publishing deals — Carry1st has signed partnerships to support the likes of Riot Games, Supercell and Activision's Call of Duty: Mobile in Africa — are not just revenue lines; they are proof-of-value demonstrations that pull the biggest studios onto the Pay1st rail and into the Carry1st Shop. Every global title that plugs in makes the storefront more indispensable to African gamers, and every African gamer who transacts makes the rail more valuable to the next studio. The flywheel is deliberately Garena-shaped: gaming acquires the user, payments monetises them, and the payments infrastructure eventually outgrows the games that seeded it.
creativeMove: The creative move is the Carry1st Shop — the consumer-facing expression of an infrastructure bet. Rather than asking African gamers to fight through checkout flows designed for American cardholders, Carry1st built a storefront where they buy gaming currency, battle passes, airtime, data and vouchers using the payment methods they actually hold. When Carry1st partnered with Supercell, the practical result was that players across Africa could buy currency and battle passes for Clash of Clans, Clash Royale, Hay Day and Brawl Stars in local currency, through local payment options, on the Carry1st Shop. The friction that had quietly excluded a continent simply disappeared.

What makes this shrewd rather than merely convenient is the merchant-of-record posture. Carry1st is not a thin payments plugin hoping to be tolerated by bigger players; it inserts itself as the accountable commercial party. That is a harder, riskier position — it owns the compliance and fraud exposure — but it is also the position that captures margin and cannot be trivially disintermediated. A publisher that has offloaded FX, tax and local compliance to Carry1st does not casually rebuild all of that in-house to save a few points. The unglamorous operational burden is precisely the moat.

The published catalogue is the demand-generation engine for the rail. By landing publishing and in-game-purchase-support relationships with Riot, Supercell and Activision — and earning recognition such as a place on Fast Company's 2024 Most Innovative Companies list — Carry1st converts brand-name IP into daily reasons for African gamers to transact on its infrastructure. The games are the bait; the payment rail is the hook. It is a genuinely elegant piece of business design: the most competitive, least ownable part of the value chain (the games) is used to build demand for the most ownable part (the rail).
africanRead: Read through a MonoKromatik lens, Carry1st is one of the cleaner examples of an African company positioning itself to own infrastructure rather than supply labour or eyeballs to someone else's platform. The reflexive African tech story is renting reach: creators feeding global platforms, developers building on foreign rails, consumers monetised by companies headquartered elsewhere. Carry1st inverts that for its core asset. Pay1st is African-built and African-owned, and being merchant of record means the company captures value on the transaction itself — not a referral fee, but a genuine cut of the flow. That is the difference between owning the toll road and being paid to wave cars through.

The honest counter-weight is authorship of the games and ownership of the equity. The titles driving traffic are global IP — Call of Duty, Clash of Clans, League of Legends — licensed and localised, not created in Africa. And the capitalisation is overwhelmingly foreign: a16z, Google, Sony, Konvoy, Bitkraft. Carry1st's corporate structure reflects the standard pattern of African startups optimised for Silicon Valley capital, which means much of the eventual financial upside flows off-continent to the funds. The rail is African; the cap table, largely, is not. Both things are true, and pretending otherwise would be the kind of PR-gloss this decode exists to strip away.

The bet that redeems the structure is control of the chokepoint. In platform economics, whoever owns the payment and distribution layer tends to outlast whoever owns any individual product on top of it. If Carry1st genuinely becomes the default way global games monetise African players, it accrues durable, compounding leverage — the ability to set terms, bundle its own products, and eventually launch African-authored titles into a distribution network it already controls. The Garena comparison is doing real work here: Sea Limited started as a games company and used the payments and commerce rails it built to become something far larger. Whether Carry1st completes that arc is unproven, and the undisclosed absolute revenues mean we should hold the celebration. But the strategic geometry — win the rail first, worry about the content later — is exactly right for a continent that has too often been sold the content and denied the rail.

lessons.title: Own the rail, not the race.
lessons.body: In any market, the hits are the most visible and least defensible asset. The durable value sits in the infrastructure the hits depend on — payments, distribution, compliance. Carry1st used games as the wedge but built its moat one layer down. Ask what everyone in your category needs but nobody wants to build, and build that.

lessons.title: Be the merchant of record, not the plugin.
lessons.body: There is a decisive difference between offering a convenient checkout and becoming the accountable commercial party. By taking on FX, tax, fraud and compliance as merchant of record, Carry1st made itself expensive to remove. The unglamorous, risky operational burden is exactly what competitors won't casually replicate — which is what makes it a moat.

lessons.title: Use the least ownable thing to sell the most ownable thing.
lessons.body: Carry1st can't own Call of Duty or Clash of Clans, so it uses them as demand-generation for the one thing it does own: the payment rail. Structure your business so the commodity part of your value chain drives traffic to the proprietary part.

lessons.title: African infrastructure and an African cap table are two different wins.
lessons.body: Building an African-owned rail is a real achievement; it does not automatically follow that the equity upside stays on the continent. Carry1st owns Pay1st but is funded largely by foreign capital. Founders raising global venture money should be clear-eyed that owning the product and owning the returns are separate battles — and plan accordingly.

title: The Brazilians: Can an African Club Own African Attention?
standfirst: Mamelodi Sundowns bought total domestic dominance and a seat at football's global table — the open question is whether winning at home converts into a brand Africans choose over Madrid and Manchester.
verificationNote: League title counts, CAF Champions League wins (2016 and 2025-26), the 2023 African Football League title, the 2025 Club World Cup group results, ownership by the Motsepe family, and Patrice Motsepe's CAF presidency are confirmed by primary and major secondary sources. Wage figures, market valuations, and sponsorship values are reported estimates that vary by outlet and currency conversion, and the club does not publish audited accounts — treat all money figures as directional, not exact.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: The strategic idea is clear and rare on the continent: fund an African club to a level where continental and global competition is the baseline expectation, not a fantasy. It is sharp locally but not novel globally — it is the same billionaire-backed dominance playbook run by PSG and Manchester City, transplanted to the PSL.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: This is the strongest axis: the club is wholly South African-owned by the Motsepe family, and the trophies, players, IP and revenue are captured on the continent rather than rented from a European platform. The moat's weakness is dependence on a single patron whose other hat — CAF president — makes the authorship harder to read as clean.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: Operationally elite by any African standard: eight consecutive league titles, two CAF Champions Leagues, the inaugural African Football League, and the first win by an African club at the expanded 32-team FIFA Club World Cup. The football machine executes at a level rivals cannot match.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: Real and double-edged. Sundowns raised the ceiling for what an African club can be and reshaped the PSL's competitive balance — but they still exited the 2025 Club World Cup at the group stage, evidence that domestic dominance does not yet convert into global brand gravity.

context: Mamelodi Sundowns are, by trophy count and financial firepower, the most dominant football club brand Africa has produced in the modern era. Founded in 1970 and based in the township of Mamelodi outside Pretoria, the club is nicknamed 'The Brazilians' — an identity borrowed decades ago when a previous owner reshaped the kit in the yellow, green and blue of Brazil's national team. That visual borrowing is worth pausing on: the most recognisable African club brand defined itself, from the start, by reference to a foreign footballing icon. The question this case study asks is whether Sundowns have since built something ownable and native, or whether the borrowing runs deeper than the shirt.

The turning point was 2004, when mining magnate Patrice Motsepe took full control of the club. Motsepe — one of South Africa's wealthiest people, whose fortune runs through African Rainbow Minerals and the Ubuntu-Botho / African Rainbow Capital investment vehicles — set an explicit goal: win the CAF Champions League, Africa's premier club competition. That goal was reached in 2016 under coach Pitso Mosimane, and again in the 2025-26 season. Domestically the dominance is close to total. Sundowns have won the South African top flight in every season from 2017-18 onward — an eight-title streak and counting — alongside a stack of domestic cups. In continental terms they became, in 2021, the first African club to hold both the men's CAF Champions League and the CAF Women's Champions League, and in 2023 they won the inaugural African Football League. In 2025 they reached the expanded FIFA Club World Cup in the United States.

The engine underneath is a patronage-plus-diversified-revenue model that no PSL rival can match. Sundowns draw from the same league broadcasting pool as everyone else — South African league TV rights are substantial by African standards — but they layer on direct corporate backing from Motsepe's businesses, premium sponsorships (a long-running Puma kit deal, a reported multi-year Ferrari sleeve partnership, Betway league sponsorship), and consistently strong match-day attendances. Reported wage figures put their top earners far above the league norm; the club does not publish audited accounts, so exact numbers are contested, but the directional truth is uncontested: Sundowns simply spend at a different altitude. In market-value league tables of African clubs they sit at or near the top, jockeying with Egypt's Al Ahly. This is the raw material of a brand. The strategic question is whether raw material has been converted into durable, ownable equity.
strategicBet: The bet is that dominance is a brand strategy. In football, unlike most categories, winning is the product and the marketing at once — a club that wins relentlessly manufactures its own highlight reel, its own narrative, its own reasons to watch. Motsepe's wager was that if you fund an African club to consistently beat its continent and then show up on the global stage, you build something that African fans will choose on merit rather than as a patriotic obligation. It is a deliberately maximalist bet in a market where most clubs are structurally under-capitalised and where the default consumption for a young South African, Nigerian or Kenyan football fan is the English Premier League, not the club down the road.

There is a sharper, less comfortable layer to the bet. Since 2021 Patrice Motsepe has been president of CAF, the body that governs the very competitions Sundowns compete in and profit from. To manage the obvious tension he handed day-to-day control of the club to his son, Tlhopie Motsepe, who now chairs it. This is a genuine strategic asset and a genuine liability at once. As an asset, it plugs the club's owning family into the commercial and governance machinery of the entire African game — no rival sits closer to the levers that set the calendar, the prize money and the media strategy of continental football. As a liability, it means every marginal refereeing call, every scheduling quirk, every prize-money decision that touches Sundowns invites a conflict-of-interest reading. A brand whose dominance is even partly attributed to proximity to power is a brand that can be argued with, and 'they only win because of who owns them' is the single most corrosive story a sports brand can carry.

The commercial logic of the bet depends on media rights and attention, not gate receipts. African club football's structural problem is that value has historically leaked to Europe: the continent's best players are sold young, its biggest fanbases spend their viewing hours and their replica-shirt money on foreign clubs, and its domestic leagues capture a fraction of the broadcast value their talent ultimately generates abroad. Sundowns' strategy is an attempt to plug that leak at one point — to build a single African club big enough to keep some of that attention, talent and money on the continent. The Club World Cup appearance is the clearest expression of the bet: a shop window in which an African club stands, for once, on the same commercial stage as Borussia Dortmund and Fluminense, in front of a global audience and global sponsors.
creativeMove: The creative move worth decoding is not a campaign — it is the decision to treat an African club as a serious, sustained investment rather than a rich man's hobby or a civic charity. Most African clubs are run hand-to-mouth or as vanity projects that spike and collapse with an owner's enthusiasm. Sundowns institutionalised the spending: a stable ownership structure, a recruitment operation that pulls the best players from across Southern Africa and beyond, continuity in coaching philosophy (the quick-passing 'Shoe Shine and Piano' style is a recognisable on-pitch signature, not just a results machine), and a women's team funded seriously enough to win its own continental title. The brand equity lives in that consistency. When a club wins for a decade without wobbling, the winning itself becomes the identity — 'Sundowns win' is now a fact the way 'Bayern win' is a fact, and that predictability is, counter-intuitively, a durable brand asset.

The second move is the yellow. The Brazilian-inspired kit is a double-edged piece of brand design. On one hand it is instantly legible — bright, warm, associated globally with beautiful, winning football, and impossible to confuse with a European club's palette. It gives Sundowns a visual identity that reads as celebratory and distinctly non-European, which matters for a brand trying to own African attention on its own terms. On the other hand, an identity built by pointing at Brazil is an identity that has outsourced its origin story. The most ownable brands author their own mythology; Sundowns' most famous nickname is, at root, a comparison. The strategic upside is that a decade of dominance and two continental titles have begun to fill 'The Brazilians' with home-grown meaning — the reference now points as much to Sundowns' own swagger as to Brazil's. Whether that transfer of meaning completes is one of the real open questions about the brand's durability.
africanRead: MonoKromatik's read is that Sundowns are the most important African club-brand experiment of the era precisely because they test, in public, whether African ownership can hold African attention against Europe. The authorship story is genuinely strong and deserves to be said plainly: this is a wholly African-owned institution that captures its value at home. The trophies, the transfer fees, the sponsorship revenue, the intellectual property of the brand — none of it is rented from a European league or a foreign platform. In a continental economy where the dominant pattern is African talent and African audiences generating value that settles overseas, a self-funded African super-club that keeps the money, the players and the glory on the continent is a structurally different and more valuable thing than another export pipeline. On the sharpest question the Index asks — who owns the value — Sundowns answer better than almost any African cultural or sporting brand of comparable scale.

But dominance and brand equity are not the same asset, and this is where the honest downside lives. Sundowns win at home almost by default, and a competition without jeopardy erodes the very drama that makes a sports brand compelling to neutrals. Domestic dominance is real, but it is dominance of a league whose commercial ceiling is a fraction of Europe's, and it is partly manufactured by a spending gap rather than earned in a fair fight — which is exactly the critique that dogs state-and-billionaire clubs everywhere. The global test was unambiguous: at the 2025 Club World Cup, Sundowns beat South Korea's Ulsan HD — the first win by an African club at the expanded 32-team tournament, a genuine milestone — then lost a seven-goal thriller to Borussia Dortmund and drew with Fluminense, finishing third in their group and going home. They competed with dignity and did not embarrass the continent. They also did not advance, and no neutral global fan converted to Sundowns fandom on the strength of it. Dominance travelled as far as respectability and stopped short of gravity.

The durability question, then, resolves into three dependencies the brand has not yet escaped. First, the patron: a brand this reliant on one family's wealth and one man's institutional position is a brand with a single point of failure, and the CAF-presidency overlap means even the club's cleanest wins carry an asterisk in the minds of rivals. Second, the ceiling: without a stronger, more competitive continental and domestic product to test against, Sundowns risk becoming very good at winning a competition too few people outside Southern Africa are watching. Third, the meaning: 'The Brazilians' is a borrowed frame that a decade of success is slowly repaying, but the brand does not yet own a native mythology as distinctive as its results. Our verdict is that Sundowns have built the most valuable African club asset of the era and the clearest proof that African ownership can compete — but that converting dominance into a brand Africans actively choose over Europe, rather than admire from a distance, is a job that is maybe half done. The trophies are the easy part. The attention is the moat, and the moat is still being dug.

lessons.title: Owning the value beats renting the reach.
lessons.body: Sundowns' real achievement is not the trophies — it is that a wholly African-owned club captures its talent, revenue and IP on the continent instead of exporting it. In a market built on value leaking to Europe, keeping the value home is the rarer and more defensible move. That is the authorship lesson every African brand-builder should copy.

lessons.title: Dominance is a product, not yet a brand.
lessons.body: Winning manufactures narrative, but a competition without jeopardy erodes the drama that makes neutrals care. Sundowns proved they can win everything at home and still fail to convert a global audience. Equity comes from being chosen, not from being unbeatable in a league few outsiders watch.

lessons.title: A single patron is a single point of failure.
lessons.body: Billionaire backing bought a decade of dominance, but a brand this dependent on one family's wealth — and one man's seat atop the governing body — carries a structural fragility and a permanent asterisk. Diversify the base of support, or the story stays 'they win because of who owns them.'

lessons.title: Borrowed identity has a repayment schedule.
lessons.body: 'The Brazilians' gave Sundowns instant legibility by pointing at someone else's icon. A decade of success is slowly transferring that meaning home, but the most durable brands author their own mythology from the start. Borrow the frame if you must — then spend relentlessly to make it yours.

title: Whose Second Act? Showmax, the Rented Platform, and the Death of an African Streamer
standfirst: MultiChoice rebuilt Africa's homegrown streamer on American technology, then handed the keys to a French owner who decided it was never worth saving.
verificationNote: Deal structure (MultiChoice 70% / NBCUniversal 30%), the February 2024 Peacock-powered relaunch, pricing tiers, loss figures and the Canal+ takeover and shutdown decision are all confirmed in primary corporate statements and multiple outlets. Precise paid-subscriber counts for Showmax were never publicly disclosed by the venture; percentage growth and migration figures are as reported by the companies and are not independently audited here.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: The 2024 relaunch thesis was coherent and current: mobile-first, 4K-capable, all-380 EPL matches at R69, local Magic-channel content on a global-grade pipe to become the number-one streamer in Africa. Sharp product logic — but the ownership architecture, renting a foreign platform, was a flaw baked into the idea itself.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: This is where the case turns. Even at relaunch the technology was Comcast's Peacock and 30% of the entity was NBCUniversal's; the pipe, the roadmap and a share of any upside were never African-owned. When Canal+ took full control it killed the product outright, with its CEO stating he would not share 30% of profits with a third party 'even if Showmax had been a success.' African value-capture was thin and is now near-zero.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: The technical relaunch was competent — 44 markets, near-100% customer migration, 88% reactivation within seven weeks, a smaller mobile app tuned for African bandwidth. But the commercial engine misfired badly: losses more than doubled to R2.6bn in FY2024 and worsened again, evidence that craft was not matched by a viable unit economics.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: MultiChoice sank more than R6bn into Showmax; the venture bled over $200m in 2025 alone, starved the parent of acquisition and retention spend as subscribers fell from 23m+ to roughly 14m, and ended with the continent's flagship homegrown streamer being switched off and folded into a Canal+ 'super app' built with OpenAI and Google. The stakes were structural.

context: Showmax launched in 2015 as MultiChoice's answer to Netflix: a Johannesburg-built streaming service for a continent that global platforms treated as an afterthought. For most of a decade it was the closest thing Africa had to a homegrown, pan-continental streamer — a South African product, carrying South African and pan-African stories, competing on a stage otherwise owned by Los Angeles and Silicon Valley.

In March 2023 that independence changed shape. MultiChoice announced a partnership with Comcast's NBCUniversal and Sky to rebuild Showmax. The structure was explicit: MultiChoice would hold 70% of the new Showmax group and NBCUniversal 30%, with a special provision giving NBCU a 23.7% indirect stake in the Nigerian subsidiary and the right to expand its holding. NBCUniversal and Sky would supply the streaming technology — Peacock's platform, which by end-2022 carried more than 20 million US paid subscribers — plus premium content licences, third-party output deals with HBO, Warner and Sony, and English Premier League rights. MultiChoice contributed the Showmax brand, a roughly 50-market footprint, and local content from Mzansi Magic, Africa Magic and Maisha Magic (Comcast press release, 2 March 2023).

The rebuilt service went live on 12 February 2024 across 44 markets in sub-Saharan Africa, running on Peacock's 4K/HDR and Atmos-ready infrastructure. The public ambition was blunt. Showmax said it wanted to 'change the game for streaming in Africa' and become 'the number one streamer' on the continent (The Hollywood Reporter). It pledged over 1,300 hours of original content a year — a 150% increase — and priced aggressively for a mobile continent: Showmax Entertainment mobile at R39 ($2.04), a Premier League mobile plan at R69 ($3.60) carrying all 380 live matches, and a reduced R89 full-entertainment tier. When prices rose in mid-2024, MultiChoice pointedly spared the Premier League plan, holding it at R69 to protect the football hook (ITWeb; TechAfrica News).

The angle that matters for MonoKromatik is not the product sheet. It is a question of authorship: when a foreign owner reboots an African streamer, who writes the second act, and who owns it? The answer that unfolded over 2024–2026 is unusually clean, and unusually uncomfortable.
strategicBet: MultiChoice's bet was that it could rent world-class technology and buy time. Building a competitive streaming stack — recommendation, live sport at scale, 4K delivery, low-bandwidth mobile — is enormously expensive, and Netflix, Amazon and Disney had a head start measured in billions. By plugging into Peacock, MultiChoice could ship a globally credible product in months rather than years, and let NBCUniversal carry the platform R&D. NBCUniversal's chairman framed the deal as a chance to 'further scale the global presence of Peacock's world-class streaming technology' — which is precisely the point: the platform's centre of gravity, and its roadmap, stayed in the United States.

This is the sovereignty trade at brand level. MultiChoice gained speed, EPL rights and premium Hollywood and Sky content; in exchange it ceded the technology layer and 30% of the entity to a foreign partner. The revenue ambition was vast — MultiChoice suggested Showmax could reach $1bn in annual revenue within five years of the relaunch. But the value chain was structurally split: African subscribers, African stories and African churn risk on one side; foreign-owned platform, foreign content licences and a foreign profit share on the other. A homegrown streamer had been re-engineered as a distribution front-end for someone else's technology. When the economics turned, MultiChoice would own the losses while the platform owner could simply decline to expand its stake.

The bet also mistook the nature of the moat. In streaming, the defensible asset is rarely the interface a subscriber sees; it is the recommendation engine, the live-sport delivery stack, the billing and identity layer, and the negotiating leverage that comes from owning the rails. Peacock's chief technology officer described the platform as 'designed from day one to deliver an exceptional experience for both on-demand and live content' across more than 70 countries — an unambiguous signal that the intelligence sat in Comcast's stack, not Showmax's. What MultiChoice retained were the two most replaceable inputs: a brand and a content catalogue. Both are real, but neither is a barrier a determined acquirer cannot walk around — as Canal+ promptly demonstrated by proposing to fold the catalogue and the audience into an entirely different, wholly-owned app and discard the Showmax shell.

There was also a timing logic that read well in early 2023 and looked worse in hindsight. Amazon had just pulled back from new African originals, and Netflix's African commissioning was cooling, which appeared to open a lane for a premium local champion. But the same macro forces squeezing the global players — currency depreciation across Nigeria and other markets, thin advertising, and subscribers who could pay only mobile-tier prices — were structural features of the African market, not a temporary gap. A strategy that depended on winning a market the giants were retreating from should have priced in why they were retreating. Renting a cost base denominated partly in dollars while collecting revenue in weakening local currencies compounded the exposure.
creativeMove: The creative and operational move was real and, on its own terms, well executed. The team compressed a global platform into an African context — hundreds of optimisations, a shrunken mobile app, tuned delivery for constrained networks — and shipped across 44 markets simultaneously. Nearly 100% of the eligible existing customer base was migrated to the new platform, and 88% of those migrated had reactivated within seven weeks of financial year-end, with record single-month growth in March 2024. The paying base grew 16% from relaunch to year-end (The Hollywood Reporter). CEO Marc Jury reduced the strategy to four verbs — compelling stories, accessible, effortless, affordable — and the football play gave the product a genuine, sticky reason to open the app daily.

But the money moved the wrong way. In the year to March 2024 revenue rose 22% to about R1.0bn ($54m) while the loss more than doubled from R1.2bn to R2.6bn ($140.5m), with a further R1.4bn poured in to chase growth. The following year was worse: a trading loss of roughly R4.9bn ($200m-plus) in 2025, an 88% deterioration, even as paying subscribers reportedly grew 44% year on year. Growth in users was not converting into a path to profit; the content bill, the EPL rights and the platform arrangement outran the low mobile ARPUs the affordability strategy depended on. Meanwhile the parent bled: MultiChoice's active base fell from over 23 million in early 2023 to around 14 million, and Canal+ would later argue that Showmax's drain forced MultiChoice to cut the very customer-acquisition and retention spend that might have slowed the decline (Business Day).

The football strategy captures the whole dilemma in miniature. English Premier League rights are the single most reliable engine of pay-TV and streaming demand across much of Africa — the reason subscribers open an app on a Saturday and the reason they resist cancelling. But those rights were an input NBCUniversal and Sky brought to the table, priced globally and denominated in hard currency, and MultiChoice was reselling them at R69 to a mobile audience. Holding that price flat through the 2024 rate rise protected the hook but widened the gap between what the content cost and what the market could pay. A brand can build an audience on borrowed rights and borrowed rails; it cannot easily build a profit on them, because the two most valuable levers — the price of the rights and the cost of the platform — are set by partners whose incentives are not identical to its own.

By the time the numbers were fully visible, the venture had also consumed the strategic attention and capital of its parent. MultiChoice put more than R6bn into Showmax over the life of the project. That is money and management focus not spent defending the legacy DStv base, which was eroding under exactly the pressure — economic squeeze, cord-cutting, piracy — that a well-funded streaming pivot was supposed to answer. The relaunch was executed as a bet-the-franchise move, and when it did not pay, it weakened the very cash engine that had been financing it.
africanRead: Then the ownership question stopped being theoretical. In September 2025 France's Canal+ completed a roughly $3bn acquisition of MultiChoice, taking control of DStv, GOtv and the whole content operation, and by October 2025 moved to a compulsory buy-out of remaining shares (Ecofin Agency; TechAfrica News). The second act of the African streamer would now be authored in Paris. And Canal+ read the balance sheet and the structure and reached a conclusion its predecessors had avoided: shut it down. CEO Maxime Saada was categorical — 'Showmax is not a commercial success. It's quite obvious' — and his CFO called the losses 'not acceptable.' Canal+ Africa's David Mignot put the number plainly: 'Showmax has been massively losing money. More than $200m just in 2025.'

The most revealing line was not about losses at all. Saada said Canal+ would not accept the ownership structure because sharing 30% of profits with a third party was unacceptable 'even if Showmax had been a success.' Read that carefully: the objection was not merely that the product lost money — it was that Canal+ would not build on a platform it did not fully own and would not split upside with NBCUniversal. That is a media-sovereignty argument, made by a French media conglomerate about an American technology partner, over the future of an African audience. Africa's largest streaming subscriber base is the prize being contested; Africa is not, in this exchange, the party doing the deciding. The plan that replaces Showmax underlines the point — a Canal+-controlled 'super app,' built with OpenAI and Google, running on technology the group owns outright. The pipe changes hands again; it does not come home.

MonoKromatik's read is that Showmax is a near-perfect case of the difference between reach and authorship. On reach, the venture succeeded — it migrated its base, grew subscribers, secured the football, shipped a premium product across the continent. On authorship it failed at inception, because the thing that makes a streamer valuable in the long run — ownership of the platform, the roadmap and the profit — was never African-held and was never going to be. When the technology is rented and 30% of the entity sits offshore, the African partner is a tenant. Tenants can be evicted. The lesson is not that MultiChoice should have refused world-class technology; it is that renting the core asset means someone else writes your last chapter. The next African streamer that matters will be judged less on its content slate than on a colder question: who owns the platform when the losses arrive?

lessons.title: Renting the platform means renting your future.
lessons.body: Speed-to-market by plugging into a foreign technology stack is a legitimate trade — but the platform layer is where long-run value and control live. If you don't own the pipe and the roadmap, you are a distribution front-end, and the owner decides when your story ends.

lessons.title: Reach is not authorship.
lessons.body: Showmax won on migration, subscriber growth and football — and still lost, because none of those metrics touch the question of who owns the asset. Measure a media brand's sovereignty by its equity in the platform and its share of profit, not by its user count.

lessons.title: A minority partner is a swing vote against you.
lessons.body: The 30% offshore stake was fatal twice: it split the upside at inception and gave the eventual acquirer a clean reason to kill the product rather than share profits. Structure foreign capital so it cannot later author the shutdown.

lessons.title: Affordability without ownership just subsidises churn.
lessons.body: R39 and R69 mobile tiers built reach on someone else's cost base. Low ARPU is survivable only when you control the platform economics; when you rent them, cheap pricing accelerates the losses that end the venture.

pullQuotes: When the technology is rented and 30% of the entity sits offshore, the African partner is a tenant. Tenants can be evicted.
The pipe changes hands again; it does not come home.
