title: Chicken Licken: How a Township Chicken Brand Out-Authored the Global Giants
standfirst: The largest non-American-owned fried-chicken franchise on earth beat KFC on cultural authorship, not media budget — and it did it while staying African-owned.
verificationNote: Founding (1981), the $1,000 Waco recipe (1972), the 1982 KFC trademark suit, the 259-outlet / R1.3bn 2013 figures, the Soweto/Alexandra township franchises, the 2018 'Legend of Big John' ARB ban, and Chicken Licken's run of Loerie 'Brand of the Year' wins are all reported by named outlets and cited below. Exact current outlet count and revenue are not independently re-verified for 2026; older published figures are dated in-text. Interpretations of authorship and strategy are MonoKromatik's, distinguished from the reported facts.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: The core idea is not 'sell chicken' — it is to make an African brand the author of the story rather than the supplier of the product. Big John 'discovering Europe' inverts the colonial map; that is a genuinely sharp strategic frame, not a jingle.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: This is the moat. Chicken Licken is family-owned, has never sold to a multinational, and owns its recipe, its IP (Soul Food, Big John, Hot Wings) and its narrative outright. It captures the brand equity it creates instead of renting a foreign master-franchise the way most global-chain outlets do.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: Two decades of Loerie recognition — including a reported seven consecutive 'Brand of the Year' wins with agency Joe Public — plus a franchise model that seeded townships first. Craft is high; the ARB ban shows the execution occasionally outran the regulator.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: A homegrown brand reached parity-adjacent scale against KFC and McDonald's in its home market and became a fixture of South African popular culture. The downside: the same brand has aggressively litigated the word 'soul' against small businesses, and a burger cannot, on its own, uplift a people.

context: Fast food in Africa is usually a story of import. The dominant chains — KFC above all — arrive as master-franchises: a foreign brand owns the name, the recipe, the marketing playbook and most of the equity, while local operators pay to run outlets and supply the labour, the rent and the risk. The reach is real, but the authorship sits overseas. Chicken Licken is the exception that proves how rare the alternative is.

George Sombonos, the son of Greek immigrants who came to South Africa during the Second World War, started young. He was working in his father's café by the age of seven and running the family roadhouse, the Dairy Den in Ridgeway, Johannesburg, on his own by twenty-three after his father's heart attack (Sunday Times obituary, 2016; Daily Investor). In 1972, touring the United States, he bought a secret fried-chicken coating recipe from an outlet owner in Waco, Texas, for one thousand US dollars — and brought it home (Wikipedia; BusinessTech).

The brand itself was born in 1981. Sombonos was about to launch a company called Golden Fried Chicken when one of his waiters suggested the name 'Chicken Licken'. He built the first outlet on the site of the old Dairy Den (Wikipedia). What followed is the part global chains could not copy: rather than chase suburban high streets, Sombonos went where the market actually was. In 1975, under apartheid's segregation laws, he had already begun serving Black customers in their cars at the roadhouse; those customers, the obituary notes, became 'the backbone of his success' (Sunday Times, 2016).

By 2013 the chain reported 259 outlets — 247 in South Africa and 12 in Botswana — selling more than 400,000 chickens and roughly five million hot wings a month, on revenue of about R1.3 billion (Wikipedia; BusinessTech). It has been described by industry sources as the largest non-American-owned fried-chicken franchise in the world, and it ranked second only to KFC in the 2007 Sunday Times Markinor Top Brands survey, with a reported market share of roughly 5% around 2010. It remains family-owned; Sombonos's daughter, Chantal Sombonos-Van Tonder, runs it as managing director and chief marketer.

The KFC contest was never hypothetical. In 1982, after Chicken Licken had opened its first township franchises, KFC sued for trademark infringement, arguing that the name sounded too close to its own 'It's finger-lickin' good' slogan. The judge disagreed, and the small local brand kept its name (Daily Investor; Entrepreneur Hub SA). It is a telling origin note: the global giant's first instinct was to litigate the upstart out of existence, and when that failed, the two would compete for decades on the one terrain the courts could not adjudicate — whose story South Africans wanted to belong to. That is the frame for everything MonoKromatik reads below.
strategicBet: Chicken Licken's strategic bet is easy to state and hard to execute: you cannot out-spend a global chain, so out-author it. KFC's parent, Yum! Brands, can put more money on more screens than any South African independent. Sombonos understood early that the winnable contest was not media weight but cultural ownership — being the brand that speaks in the audience's own voice, about the audience's own world, from a position the multinational structurally cannot occupy.

The first move in that bet was distribution, not advertising. When KFC and its peers were courting suburban, historically white shopping precincts, Chicken Licken planted itself in the townships. Early franchises in Soweto and Alexandra (1982) were reportedly given away, with no royalties charged in the opening months, to accelerate Black entrepreneurial ownership of outlets and put the brand at the centre of township daily life (BusinessTech). That is authorship expressed as geography: the brand grew from the majority market outward, rather than treating it as an afterthought.

The second, and sharper, part of the bet is that the value created by that cultural fluency should stay in-house. Chicken Licken never sold to a multinational. It owns its recipe, its trademarks — Soul Food, Full House, Hot Wings, Popcorn Chicken, Big John — and, crucially, its own advertising narrative, developed over years with a single South African agency, Joe Public. Where a KFC franchisee rents a foreign playbook, Chicken Licken writes its own and keeps the copyright. In MonoKromatik's read, that combination of owned IP, owned narrative and owned equity is the whole game; the chicken is almost incidental.

The discipline of that bet is worth dwelling on, because most challengers abandon it under pressure. The obvious growth move for a successful African fast-food brand is to sell a controlling stake to a global operator in exchange for capital and international scale — and to adopt the acquirer's centralised, globally-templated marketing in the bargain. That is the moment authorship is quietly surrendered. Sombonos never took it. He kept the company closely held, kept marketing decisions in Johannesburg, and let the brand grow at the pace its own cash flow and franchise network allowed. Slower, yes; but every increment of brand equity it built stayed sovereign. The bet, in one line, is that a smaller pie you fully own beats a slice of a larger pie whose recipe someone else controls.
creativeMove: The clearest expression of the strategy is the 2018 campaign 'The Legend of Big John', created by Joe Public. It tells, as oral history, the tale of a young Black African man who in 1650 sets out alone across treacherous oceans, survives sea-monsters and beasts, and 'discovers' a foreign land he names 'Eu-rope'. The Big John is a real menu item; the film gave it a mythology that quietly reversed the entire colonial script of discovery — Africa as author and explorer, Europe as the thing found (Ads of the World; Quartz Africa).

It was too sharp for the regulator. Just weeks after release, on 18 December 2018, the Advertising Regulatory Board banned the ad after a single complaint, ruling that it trivialised colonialism: 'Atrocities suffered by Africans under colonization are well documented... This experience can never be rewritten differently and cannot be trivialized in any manner' (OkayAfrica; Quartz Africa). The ban became the story — free national coverage, a debate about who gets to narrate history, and a brand positioned unmistakably on the side of African imagination. A follow-up, 'Big John Beats Ya'hunga' (2022), extended the world with a Black Panther / Wakanda parody launched on the film's opening day.

Big John sits inside a longer body of work. The brand's 'Soul' platform — Soul Food for a Soul Nation, and later the #SoulFood2TheWorld idea of a world running 'dangerously low on soul' — frames the product as cultural nourishment rather than calories. This is the through-line from the 1986 Joe Mafela jingle ('it's good, good, good, it's good it's nice') to today: Chicken Licken consistently talks about belonging, pride and Blackness, not about price or crispiness. The commercial results back the craft — Chicken Licken has been a repeat Loerie 'Brand of the Year', reported at seven consecutive wins with Joe Public, an unprecedented run in recent South African advertising (Bizcommunity / Joe Public).

What makes the creative move genuinely hard to copy is that it is not one great ad but a sustained authorial voice. Global chains localise — they take a globally-set brief and adapt it to a market. Chicken Licken originates: the ideas start from a South African vantage, in South African languages and registers, aimed at making the audience feel authored-for rather than marketed-to. The Mafela jingle, the Soul platform and the Big John mythology are not disconnected campaigns but chapters of the same long argument that this brand belongs to the people watching it. That continuity — one agency, one owner, one voice, across nearly four decades — is itself a strategic asset a rotating roster of global-network agencies structurally cannot reproduce.
africanRead: Read from the continent, Chicken Licken matters less as a chicken business than as a proof: an African-owned, African-authored brand can beat the global incumbents at the one thing budget cannot buy — being of the culture rather than marketing to it. KFC will always have more money; it will never have Big John. The authorship advantage is not decorative. It is the reason a family firm from Ridgeway can hold a place in the national imagination that a multinational, however well-funded, cannot manufacture. This is the MonoKromatik thesis in one brand: reach can be rented, authorship must be owned, and owned authorship is the durable moat. Note too that the authorship began before the advertising: serving Black customers in 1975, and seeding township franchises in 1982, meant that by the time the brand spoke in the culture's voice it had already earned the standing to do so. The cultural authorship was credible precisely because the commercial relationship came first — pride the brand had banked, not borrowed.

It is also proof that value-capture is a design choice. The default African fast-food story hands the equity abroad through the master-franchise model. Sombonos refused that trade twice over — he kept the company family-owned, and he built the brand's meaning in-house rather than importing it. When Chicken Licken wins a Loerie, the reputational capital compounds for a South African company; when a global chain runs a great local ad, the equity ultimately accrues to a balance sheet in another hemisphere. That difference is the entire argument for African authorship as strategy, not sentiment.

The honest downside must be stated, because a decode that only flatters is not intelligence. First, cultural pride here is doing commercial work: the Africa Is A Country critic Duane Jethro grants that Big John 'generates a postcolonial imaginary space' for reimagining Black historical agency — and, in the same breath, that his actual burger was 'a salty, soggy mess', and that a burger cannot liberate anyone. Decolonial imagery sells product; that is a real tension, not a resolved one. Second, the brand that built itself on 'Soul' has repeatedly litigated the word 'soul' against far smaller businesses, including a 2019 case it lost against a vegan restaurant, Oh My Soul. Owning your authorship is the moat; over-policing it against the small is where the same instinct curdles. MonoKromatik's score rewards the authorship and the consequence while naming the cost.

lessons.title: Out-author, don't out-spend.
lessons.body: You will rarely beat a global incumbent on media budget. You can beat it on authorship — being genuinely of the culture, speaking in its voice, telling stories a foreign balance sheet cannot originate. Chicken Licken's Big John is worth more than the media weight KFC can buy because KFC can never own it.

lessons.title: Own the IP or you own nothing.
lessons.body: The master-franchise model hands equity abroad. Chicken Licken kept the recipe, the trademarks and the narrative in-house and stayed family-owned. When your brand equity compounds, make sure it compounds onto your own balance sheet, not someone else's.

lessons.title: Serve the majority market first, not last.
lessons.body: Growth followed the customer. Seeding township franchises before chasing suburbs put the brand at the centre of the largest market's daily life — a distribution decision that made the later cultural authority credible rather than borrowed.

lessons.title: A ban can be a billboard — but pride is not a product.
lessons.body: The ARB ban amplified Big John into a national conversation Chicken Licken could never have bought. Yet cultural pride doing commercial work is a real tension: the imagery liberates the imagination; the burger is still a burger. Wield the meaning, but do not confuse selling it with delivering it.

pullQuotes: KFC will always have more money. It will never have Big John.
Reach can be rented. Authorship must be owned — and owned authorship is the moat.

title: Kenneth Ize: Owning the Loom, Not Just the Label
standfirst: A Nigerian designer built a global fashion house on handwoven aso-oke he controls from the loom up — a test of whether African craft can be scaled by its author rather than licensed into someone else's luxury.
verificationNote: Confirmed via press and reference sources: 2019 LVMH Prize finalist, Feb 2020 Paris debut with Naomi Campbell, Ilorin weaving operation of 10–15 weavers, the 2021 Karl Lagerfeld SS21 capsule, the 2022 split from investor IFFAC and label hiatus, and the Fall 2023 upcycled-collection return. Financial figures (~€520,000 invested by/via IFFAC; 'almost half a million euros' in sales) are as reported by WWD in Ize's own words and not independently audited. The 'first Black designer to collaborate with the Karl Lagerfeld maison' claim is widely reported, not company-confirmed here.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: Take aso-oke — a Yoruba prestige cloth largely confined to ceremony — and build both a contemporary global silhouette and the weaving infrastructure to supply it. The originality is not the fabric but the decision to own its production rather than source it.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: Ize owns the house, the name, and the loom: fabric is woven by a Nigerian team he employs in Ilorin, not bought finished. That vertical craft ownership is the moat — but the 2022 investor split exposed how thin the capital under that ownership was.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: The craft and the runway were world-class — Paris, Naomi Campbell, a V&A acquisition, LVMH and Woolmark shortlists. The business operations were not: lost shipments, unfulfilled orders on 'almost half a million euros' of sales, and a full hiatus by 2022.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: He put Nigerian handweaving on the global luxury map, employed and trained weavers, and reframed aso-oke as high fashion. The hiatus is the cautionary half of the consequence: the impact is real but its financial base proved fragile.

context: Kenneth Ize was born in Lagos on 5 October 1990 and moved to Austria at the age of four. He studied at the University of Applied Arts Vienna under Bernhard Willhelm and Hussein Chalayan, then launched his eponymous label at Lagos Fashion Week after graduating in 2013, relaunching in 2015 after a master's degree. That biography matters: Ize is a diaspora designer who chose to route his brand's value back through Nigeria rather than through the European ateliers that trained him.

The material at the centre of the house is aso-oke — a handwoven cloth of Yoruba origin, traditionally worn for weddings, chieftaincy and other high-status occasions. Aso-oke is not a print or a motif that can be reproduced on a mill loom; it is a labour-intensive strip-weave made on narrow looms, historically a marker of prestige precisely because of the hours embedded in it. Ize's move was to lift this cloth out of the ceremonial economy and into a contemporary, gender-neutral, internationally-sold ready-to-wear line — clean tailoring and flowing silhouettes cut from stripes and checks that read as both ancestral and modern.

Crucially, Ize did not license the look of aso-oke onto factory fabric. He produces the cloth itself with a community of roughly 10 to 15 weavers at a facility in Ilorin, in western Nigeria, and has spoken of building a centre there that doubles as a production unit and a training site — with an ambition to bring weaving into the Nigerian school curriculum. As he told the press, 'It takes a person to create the fabric they are made from, and it takes days to make, within a community, weaving the cloth. It's their life and DNA.' The supply chain is not a sourcing arrangement; it is the product.

The distinction is worth labouring because it is where most 'African luxury' stories quietly break down. A great many designers, African and otherwise, take a heritage motif — a print, a check, a weave pattern — and have it reproduced on industrial fabric sourced from a mill in Europe or Asia. The reference is African; the manufacturing, the margin and the intellectual property are not. Ize's decision to weave the actual cloth, from raw materials, with a named team he pays, moves the value chain in the opposite direction. It also imposes a discipline the print route never does: he cannot simply reorder more fabric to meet a spike in demand, because the constraint is human hours on narrow looms, not machine capacity. Slow fashion, in his hands, is not a marketing adjective; it is a structural fact of how the cloth exists.

This is why Kenneth Ize sits naturally alongside Thebe Magugu and MaXhosa Africa's Laduma Ngxokolo in MonoKromatik's fashion-authorship set. All three are African designers who own their houses and root the value in a specific local craft or archive — Magugu in South African storytelling and print, Ngxokolo in Xhosa knitwear, Ize in Yoruba weaving. The Ize case is the sharpest test of the model's most demanding version: not just owning the brand, but owning the means of making the cloth. Where Magugu authors the narrative and Ngxokolo authors the knit, Ize authors the raw material itself — which is both the deepest form of the moat and, as the business would learn, the most capital-intensive.
strategicBet: The bet is vertical: control the loom, and you control the story, the margin, and the moat. Anyone can be inspired by aso-oke; almost no one selling globally actually manufactures it at scale under their own roof in Nigeria. By employing weavers directly and building toward a training facility, Ize positioned the brand so that its scarcest input — skilled hands and time — sits inside the company rather than being bought from a market he doesn't control. In luxury, that is the classic argument for a maison: own the atelier, own the value.

The validating signals arrived fast. In 2019 Ize was a finalist for the LVMH Prize — among the first African designers to reach that stage — and in February 2020 he staged his Paris Fashion Week debut with Naomi Campbell and Imaan Hammam on the runway. He was later an International Woolmark Prize finalist and, in December 2020, a Fashion Awards honoree in the community category. A Spring/Summer 2021 look was acquired by London's Victoria and Albert Museum. For a house built on a single Nigerian craft, this was extraordinary institutional endorsement in under two years.

But the bet carried a hidden liability that the awards obscured: owning production is capital-hungry and unforgiving. A weaving facility must be paid whether or not orders convert to cash, and handwoven cloth cannot be scaled by simply placing a larger factory order. The strategic strength — vertical craft ownership — was also the strategic exposure. When the working capital behind it failed, the very thing that made the house distinctive became the thing that could sink it.
creativeMove: The most instructive move for this analysis is the one that looks most like a triumph: the July 2021 Karl Lagerfeld x Kenneth Ize capsule. It was a genuine milestone — widely reported as the first time a Black designer collaborated with the Karl Lagerfeld maison — and it put aso-oke references onto a European luxury brand's global retail footprint, co-designed with Lagerfeld design director Hun Kim, priced roughly $120–$825, gender-neutral, sold through Karl Lagerfeld's channels.

Read through the authorship lens, the collaboration is the counter-model to Ize's own house. In the capsule, aso-oke is present as inspiration — patterns and pops of colour translated into Karl Lagerfeld's black-and-white signature and its supply chain, its stores, its brand equity. That is the licensing path: African craft rents its aesthetic to a European platform, gains reach and validation, and leaves the ownership where it started. Ize's standalone label is the opposite bet — the craft, the cloth, the name and the margin all held by an African-owned house. The same designer ran both experiments almost simultaneously, which is what makes the case unusually legible: it shows exactly what is gained (reach, cash, prestige) and what is not captured (the underlying value) when heritage is licensed rather than owned.

It would be too easy to read the collaboration as a compromise; it was, on its own terms, a smart use of a large platform, and the 'first Black designer to work with the maison' framing carried real symbolic weight for who gets to sit inside European luxury at all. The point is narrower and sharper: a capsule is a transaction, not a foundation. It monetises the aesthetic without transferring the manufacturing base, the training pipeline or the equity to the African side. For a designer trying to build a durable house, the collaboration can subsidise the real work but cannot substitute for it — and the events of 2022 would show, painfully, that the real work was the independent label and its loom in Ilorin, not the co-branded rail in a Paris store. The prestige of the collaboration and the fragility of the house existed at the same moment, in the same person.
africanRead: MonoKromatik's read is that Kenneth Ize built the right thing and nearly lost it for the wrong reasons — and that the near-loss is the most valuable lesson in African fashion authorship. The house is a model of what value-capture should look like: the loom is in Nigeria, the weavers are employed, the cloth is proprietary in practice, and the name on the door is the author's. That is materially different from a designer who prints an 'African-inspired' motif on mill fabric and books the margin abroad. On authorship, Ize scores high because he owns the hardest-to-own part of the chain.

The honest downside is that ownership without patient, aligned capital is fragile. By 2022 Ize had parted ways with his investor — Roberta Annan's Impact Fund for African Creatives (IFFAC), into which he told WWD roughly €520,000 had gone — and placed the label on hiatus. In his own words, 'We made almost half a million euros... and I can't produce that, and get more money into the business.' He described plugging personal savings into the Nigerian production facility to keep it alive, and a run of operational failures — UPS losing two shipments, an Italian partner not paying. Demand was not the problem; the machinery to convert demand into fulfilled orders and reinvested cash was. He returned for Fall 2023 in Paris with a deliberately personal collection assembled from upcycled Lagos street-market clothing, and set up the Kenneth Ize NGO to finance local production and training.

The strategic verdict for African brand-builders is therefore two-sided. First, vertical craft ownership is a real and rare moat — it is what separates a fashion author from a fashion stylist, and it is why Ize belongs in the Magugu/MaXhosa lane rather than the parade of designers who license the look and lose the value. Second, that moat is only as strong as the capital structure beneath it: owning production means owning fixed cost, cash-flow risk and logistics risk, and it demands investors who understand that handweaving cannot be scaled like a spreadsheet. The Karl Lagerfeld capsule delivered reach and prestige with none of that operational burden — which is precisely why it could not, on its own, build a durable African-owned house. The reach was rented; the risk, and the ownership, stayed with the independent label.

lessons.title: Own the loom, not just the logo.
lessons.body: The difference between a fashion author and a fashion stylist is who controls the scarcest input. Ize employs weavers and produces his own aso-oke in Nigeria, so the value lives inside an African-owned house rather than being licensed abroad. If your brand is built on a craft, the strategic question is not whether you reference it but whether you make it.

lessons.title: A rented platform buys reach, not ownership.
lessons.body: The Karl Lagerfeld capsule gave Ize global prestige and cash flow with no operational burden — and captured none of the underlying value in a European brand's stores. Licensing your heritage is a legitimate accelerant, but it is not house-building. Know which one you are doing, and never mistake the reach for the moat.

lessons.title: Vertical ownership is a fixed cost, so raise for it accordingly.
lessons.body: Owning production means owning payroll, logistics and cash-flow risk that a wholesale designer never touches. Ize could sell 'almost half a million euros' and still stall because the capital behind the loom wasn't patient or aligned. If the moat is manufacturing, the fundraising has to match the moat — investors who understand that handwork cannot be scaled like software.

lessons.title: Craft acclaim and operational health are different scoreboards.
lessons.body: LVMH, Woolmark, the V&A and Naomi Campbell all validated the work while the business quietly ran out of runway. Awards measure the idea and the execution of the object; they say nothing about fulfilment, working capital or logistics. Track both, and never let the trophy shelf hide the balance sheet.

pullQuotes: Anyone can be inspired by aso-oke; almost no one selling globally actually weaves it under their own roof in Nigeria.
The reach was rented; the risk, and the ownership, stayed with the independent label.

title: OPay Owns the Everyday Naira — But Not the Upside
standfirst: A Chinese-founded, SoftBank-funded wallet became the default way Nigerians move money; the reach is Nigerian, the equity is not.
verificationNote: Valuations, funding rounds, ownership structure, user/agent figures and transaction values are drawn from company statements, Opera's public filings and reputable press; some usage figures (daily active users, agent counts, transaction success rates) are company-reported and not independently audited. Internal revenue, deposit balances and profit for OPay are not publicly disclosed and are not claimed here.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: Betting early and hard on a cashless Nigeria — building resilient rails and a physical agent army ahead of demand — was a sharp, prescient call. But the playbook is imported wholesale from China's Alipay/WeChat super-app model, not invented for the market.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: This is the fault line. OPay was founded by Chinese billionaire Zhou Yahui via Opera and scaled on SoftBank and Sequoia China money; Nigerians supply the deposits, transactions and last-mile distribution, while the equity upside accrues to Opera and its foreign backers. Reach is Nigerian; ownership of the rails is not.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: Operationally elite. When Nigeria's bank apps buckled during the 2023 cash crunch and later outages, OPay's infrastructure held, its 500,000-plus agents kept cash flowing, and it became the single most-downloaded app in the country.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: Enormous and structural. OPay and PalmPay drove mobile-money value to ₦20.71 trillion in a single quarter, banked millions of first-time users, and durably rewired how everyday Nigeria pays — a genuine shift in the country's financial plumbing.

context: In the first quarter of 2025, mobile-money transactions in Nigeria reached ₦20.71 trillion — about $13.49 billion — a figure that had multiplied more than fifteen-fold since early 2021 (TechCabal, citing NIBSS data). Two names sit at the centre of that surge, and neither was founded by a Nigerian: OPay and PalmPay. Between them they process the daily rituals of Nigerian economic life — the transfer to a trader, the airtime top-up, the POS withdrawal at a roadside kiosk — at a scale that now dwarfs many incumbent banks. This is the record of how the everyday naira came to run on foreign-capital rails.

OPay is the anchor of that story. It launched its payments service in Nigeria in August 2018, spun out of Opera — the browser company — and Balder Investment, an entity controlled by Opera's executive chairman, the Chinese billionaire Zhou Yahui (TechCrunch, 2019). Its early incarnation was a blitzscaling super-app: a wallet bolted to a motorcycle-hailing service (ORide), food delivery (OFood) and more, chasing a million orders a day on the back of heavy subsidy. When COVID and a regulatory crackdown on okada bikes gutted those verticals in 2020, OPay stripped itself back to what worked — payments — and rebuilt around wallets, transfers, and a vast agent network.

The timing proved extraordinary. In late 2022 Nigeria's central bank redesigned the naira and imposed withdrawal limits; poor execution triggered a cash crisis that, by February 2023, had cut currency in circulation to its lowest level since 2008. As bank apps crashed and ATMs ran dry, Nigerians reached for whatever still worked — and OPay worked. By March 2023 it was among the most-downloaded finance apps in the country; by October it was the single most-downloaded app of any kind, with more than 26 million members and reporting, in the words of then co-CEO Olu Akanmu, 'some of the strongest growth in our history' (TechCabal, 2023). Its rival PalmPay — founded in 2019 and backed by the Chinese phone maker Transsion and NetEase — rode the same wave, and today reports over 35 million registered users (Vanguard, 2026).
strategicBet: OPay's core bet was that peer-to-peer, agent-assisted digital payments would become the default for a country the formal banking system had never fully reached — and that whoever built the most resilient rails before the demand arrived would own the moment when it did. That is a capital-intensive, patience-heavy wager, and it was funded accordingly. In 2021 OPay raised $400 million in a round led by SoftBank's Vision Fund 2 with Sequoia Capital China participating, vaulting to a $2 billion valuation and the title of Africa's fastest unicorn (World Economic Forum, 2021). Opera's stake, disclosed in its public filings, has since been marked up to imply an OPay valuation of roughly $2.75 billion (Semafor, 2024).

The second, quieter bet was distribution as a moat. Digital reach in Nigeria is throttled by the last mile — the point where a wallet balance must become physical cash and back again. OPay answered with agents: by 2023 it claimed more than 500,000 of them, small operators with POS terminals turning street corners into cash-in/cash-out points. PalmPay layered on a distribution edge OPay could not easily match — Transsion, which commands over 40% of Africa's smartphone market through Tecno and Infinix, pre-installs PalmPay on select financed handsets, seeding the app onto millions of devices before a user has chosen anything (TechCrunch, 2025). In both cases the strategic insight is the same: in a cash-heavy, thin-margin market, the winner is whoever is physically closest to the transaction.

The bet has paid, commercially. PalmPay is now reported to be profitable, with 2023 revenue of about $64 million that has since more than doubled, and is in talks to raise up to $100 million to expand across Africa and into Asia (TechCrunch, 2025). OPay does not disclose its financials, but its trajectory — a national microfinance-bank licence, a valuation near $3 billion, and persistent IPO signals from Opera — points the same way. The rails are being monetised. The question MonoKromatik presses is where the monetisation lands.

There is a third bet worth naming: capital that could outlast the losing years. Blitzscaling a payments network means years of subsidised transfers, agent incentives and thin-to-negative margins before the flywheel spins. Nigerian venture capital, in 2018-2021, was neither deep enough nor patient enough to fund that curve at the required scale; the cheques that were, came from SoftBank, Sequoia China and Opera. That is the mechanism by which foreign ownership entered the everyday naira — not through a hostile takeover, but through the simple fact that the people willing to lose money for five years to own the rails were not Nigerian. Understanding that is the first step to changing it: the constraint was never Nigerian talent or demand, it was the depth and patience of local capital.
creativeMove: The craft here is not in a campaign or a logo; it is in operational design, and it is genuinely impressive. OPay's defining creative move was to treat reliability as the product. While incumbent banks treated digital as a channel bolted onto branch infrastructure, OPay engineered for the failure case — the assumption that the network would be stressed, the counterparty unbanked, and the transaction small. PalmPay reports a 99.5% transaction success rate and 15 million daily transactions (TechCabal); OPay reports tens of millions of daily active users. Those numbers are company-supplied and unaudited, but the lived experience during the 2023 cash crunch corroborated the direction: the apps that stayed up won the country.

The second move was to make the agent a brand surface. The green OPay umbrella and the branded POS stand are now visual furniture of Nigerian streets — a physical presence that doubles as marketing, onboarding desk, and cash machine. This is a deliberate inversion of the fintech convention that everything should be in-app; OPay understood that in Nigeria the app is only as strong as the human standing next to a cash drawer. It is a design lesson African brand-builders should study closely: the interface that matters most may be the one made of people, plastic signage and a working POS, not the screen.

What OPay did not do is equally instructive. It did not try to be a lifestyle brand or lean on cultural cachet; it competed on uptime, spread and price. That discipline is why it survived the super-app cull of 2020 and why it was ready when the cash crisis handed it a market. The move is copyable in its logic — resilience plus distribution — but expensive to execute, which is precisely why it has been financed from abroad.

There is craft, too, in pricing and incentive design that most observers miss. OPay and PalmPay bought their early user bases with aggressive subsidies — free or near-free transfers, cash-back on airtime, referral bonuses — a deliberate loss leader to make the wallet the default before charging for the layers above it. It is the classic platform sequence: subsidise the commodity transaction to own the customer, then earn on lending, merchant services and float. That the sequence is now visibly working — PalmPay profitable, OPay eyeing an IPO — is the clearest sign that the land-grab phase is closing and the harvest phase is opening. Whoever owns the platform at the start of the harvest owns the years of margin that follow, which is exactly why the ownership question is not academic but time-sensitive.
africanRead: Here is the uncomfortable centre of the file. On every axis of reach, OPay and PalmPay are Nigerian success stories: Nigerian users, Nigerian agents, Nigerian transactions, Nigerian financial inclusion — a quarter of PalmPay's users say it was their first-ever financial account. But on the axis that MonoKromatik weights most heavily — authorship, meaning who shaped and who OWNS the value — the picture inverts. OPay was founded and is chaired by a Chinese billionaire, incubated by a Chinese-controlled Norwegian-listed company (Opera), and scaled on Japanese (SoftBank) and Chinese (Sequoia China) capital. PalmPay is a Transsion/NetEase creation. The deposits, the network effects and the daily transaction fees are generated in Nigeria; the equity that those fees revalue upward sits on cap tables in the Cayman Islands, Tokyo and Beijing.

This is not a moral indictment of the founders — building resilient payment rails is hard, capital-intensive work, and foreign investors took real risk when local ones would not. It is a structural observation about value capture. When Opera marks its OPay stake up by tens of millions of dollars in a quarterly filing, that gain is a claim on the future cash flows of Nigerian commerce, and it belongs to Opera's shareholders. The naira moves through rails Nigerians built with their transactions and their agent labour; the appreciation on those rails is booked abroad. Reach without ownership is a familiar African pattern — in extractives, in telecoms, in music streaming — and fintech has now reproduced it at the most intimate layer of the economy: how people pay each other.

The strategic stakes for Nigeria are real. Payments data is a strategic asset; the operator who sees every transaction can build the credit, insurance and commerce layers on top — and those higher-margin layers are where the durable value sits. If that stack is foreign-owned, Nigeria has outsourced not just its rails but the intelligence riding on them, and its regulators (the CBN, which licenses these players as microfinance banks and mobile-money operators) hold less leverage than the transaction volumes imply. The counter-case — argued by the companies and not without merit — is that inclusion delivered is worth more than ownership withheld, that millions banked for the first time is a public good regardless of the cap table, and that local challengers like Moniepoint and Paga are proof the market is still contestable by Nigerian capital.

MonoKromatik's read: OPay is an A-grade operating company and a C-grade answer to the ownership question, and Nigeria should hold both truths at once. The reach is admirable and the inclusion is real. But a country whose everyday payments run on foreign-owned rails has won the convenience and rented the sovereignty. The unfinished work — for local founders, local capital and the state — is not to replicate OPay's app but to own more of the next layer: the credit, the data, the equity. Reach is table stakes. Ownership is the game.

lessons.title: Reach is not ownership — score them separately.
lessons.body: OPay dominates how Nigerians pay while the equity upside accrues abroad. When you assess an African champion, do not let impressive usage numbers stand in for value capture; ask who owns the cap table and who books the appreciation.

lessons.title: In cash-heavy markets, distribution is the product.
lessons.body: OPay's 500,000 agents and PalmPay's Transsion pre-installs beat slicker apps because they solved the last mile — cash-in, cash-out, and a human next to the transaction. Build the physical layer, not just the screen.

lessons.title: Engineer for the failure case.
lessons.body: OPay won the 2023 cash crunch because it treated reliability as the product and built resilient rails before demand arrived. When incumbents' systems buckled, uptime — not branding — decided the market.

lessons.title: Own the next layer, not just the rails.
lessons.body: Payments generate the data that powers credit, insurance and commerce — the higher-margin stack. For African founders and capital, the unfinished work is not another wallet but owning the intelligence and equity that ride on top of it.

title: The Pipe Wants to Own the Story: MTN's Third Run at African Streaming
standfirst: MTN can't out-spend Netflix on content — but it owns the billing relationship and the mobile-money rails, which may be the only genuinely African-owned route into media distribution.
verificationNote: Confirmed from MTN's own results, launch communications and multiple outlets: the June 2026 One TV launch, the Synamedia technology partnership, airtime/MoMo payment support, and the 2025 group metrics (307m customers, 70m MoMo users, 23bn+ transactions, US$500bn+ transaction value). MusicTime's launch and 'modest' traction are reported; exact subscriber counts and One TV pricing are not disclosed. The strategic argument — that the billing relationship and fintech rails are MTN's most defensible asset in media — is MonoKromatik interpretation, not an MTN claim. MTN's Ambition 2030 does NOT list media/entertainment as a named platform; it names Connectivity, Fintech and Digital Infrastructure.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: The sharp move is not 'a telco makes a Netflix.' It is recognising that in markets where 45% of your customers have never used the internet and most have no credit card, the payment rail — airtime deduction and mobile money — is the scarce asset, not the catalogue. Framing content as the 'front door to the digital economy' priced in the wallet Africans already use is a genuinely strong read of the terrain.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: MTN owns the two things global platforms cannot buy: the billing relationship with 307m customers and 70m mobile-money wallets. That is real African-owned value-capture at the distribution and payment layer. But the video technology is Synamedia (UK), and the culture itself — the music and film — is still authored and largely owned by creators and licensors. MTN is building the toll-road and the till, not the story that travels on them.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: This is attempt three. MTN VU (2014–2017) closed; the 2023 Prime Video Mobile Edition partner, Amazon, exited Africa in 2024; MusicTime found only modest traction. One TV launched cleanly on a credible cloud stack across a phased rollout, and the fintech integration is the real operational moat — but the graveyard of telco streaming (Kwese TV, Cell C's Black, Vodacom's Video Play) is a warning that reach has never been the hard part.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: If MTN makes airtime-and-MoMo the default way 300m+ Africans pay for entertainment, it becomes the gatekeeper — and potentially the price-setter — for how the continent accesses media, capturing margin that currently leaks to card networks and foreign platforms. The downside is equally material: a fourth failure would confirm that owning the pipe does not let you own the audience.

context: MTN Group is Africa's largest mobile operator: 307 million customers across 16 markets at the end of 2025, R218 billion in service revenue, and a fintech arm — MoMo — with roughly 70 million active users processing more than 23 billion transactions worth over US$500 billion a year. It is, by any measure, one of the most important pieces of infrastructure on the continent. It is also, structurally, a business that has spent two decades laying pipe while the most valuable traffic flowing through that pipe — Netflix, YouTube, Amazon, Spotify, TikTok — is owned by companies headquartered thousands of kilometres away. Every hour an MTN customer spends inside one of those apps is an hour MTN carries at cost and monetises only at the thin margin of a data bundle.

That asymmetry is the whole story. MTN builds and maintains the network at enormous capital cost — R38 billion in network investment in 2025 alone — while global platforms monetise the attention that network carries. And the commodity MTN sells to fund it, the data bundle, is a deflating asset: average data prices fell 14% for customers in 2025 even as consumption climbed to 12.5GB a month per user and total data traffic rose 27%. The operator is running to stand still, cutting the price of the exact thing it sells so that customers can consume more of someone else's product. This is the classic 'dumb pipe' trap made concrete — a utility that carries everyone else's value and captures almost none of it — and it is the specific fear that a content strategy is meant to answer.

The pressure has intensified because the African content market is consolidating around a foreign owner. In September 2025, France's Canal+ completed its roughly US$2 billion (R35 billion) takeover of MultiChoice — the DStv and Showmax parent — combining francophone leadership with anglophone and lusophone dominance to reach more than 40 million subscribers across nearly 70 countries, and targeting over €400 million of EBITDA synergies by 2030. In other words, at the very moment MTN moves toward content, the continent's largest pay-TV and streaming asset has passed into European hands. If MTN does not build a distribution position of its own, the future of how Africans pay for African stories is a negotiation between a French media group and a handful of Silicon Valley platforms.

So in June 2026 MTN launched One TV, a streaming platform built with UK video-technology firm Synamedia (a partnership first announced in April 2025), rolling out across its markets from South Africa and Nigeria outward — the Nigeria launch dated to 9 June 2026. It bundles live channels, local productions and international programming under free ad-supported, pay-per-view and subscription tiers, all payable by airtime deduction, MoMo wallet or, in some markets, bank card. In parallel, MTN Nigeria has begun courting the music industry: a May 2026 Lagos workshop, 'Reverberation: The Blueprint for Africa's Digital Audio Future,' signalled a coming platform pitched on revenue transparency and artist data. As Chief Digital Officer A'isha Mumuni put it, MTN is 'eager to re-enter the space, but with a fresh approach.'

The word 're-enter' is doing heavy lifting. This is not MTN's first content ambition, or its second. MTN VU launched in South Africa in 2014 with Hollywood studio deals and free-data sweeteners, and shut down in 2017. In 2023 MTN Nigeria fronted Amazon's Prime Video Mobile Edition — and Amazon pulled back from Africa the following year, stranding the partnership. MusicTime, the time-based music service where customers buy blocks of streaming time rather than a monthly subscription, is the one survivor, and even it is described in the trade press as only a 'modest' success. One TV is therefore the third serious run at the same wall, launched into a market that has already buried a row of telco streamers — Kwese TV, Cell C's Black, Vodacom's Video Play — that had scale and still failed.
strategicBet: The bet is not that MTN can out-produce or out-license Netflix. It cannot, and it is not pretending to. The bet is that the point of maximum leverage in African media is not the content — it is the checkout. This is a real, documented constraint, not a slogan: subscription payments in Africa are structurally hard because card penetration is low and recurring card billing fails at high rates, which is why global services increasingly lean on direct carrier billing. Netflix itself already lets Vodacom South Africa customers charge their subscription to airtime or a postpaid bill precisely because the card rail excludes so many otherwise-willing buyers. MTN's insight is to stop treating that rail as a grudging add-on and make it the front door: One TV is priced in airtime and MoMo from day one, in denominations a customer can afford daily rather than monthly.

This is where the Ambition 2030 framing matters, and where MTN is quietly more honest than its marketing. The group's stated strategy names three platforms: Connectivity, Fintech and Digital Infrastructure. Media and entertainment is conspicuously not on the list. Read correctly, that omission is the tell — MTN does not see content as a business in itself. It sees content as a use-case that pulls the two platforms it actually intends to own: data (connectivity) and MoMo (fintech). Selorm Adadevoh, the group's chief commercial, strategy and transformation officer, said the quiet part plainly: entertainment is becoming 'an important gateway to digital participation,' and One TV 'leverages the scale of our connectivity, fintech and digital capabilities.' Streaming is the bait; the wallet is the hook. A customer who tops up airtime to watch a match, then leaves that top-up habit behind in a MoMo wallet, is worth far more to MTN than the pay-per-view fee alone.

The economics of that bet are brutal for anyone playing streaming as a pure content business — which is precisely why MTN's angle is more defensible than a straight comparison to Netflix suggests. Independent analysis of African streaming is blunt: the unit economics do not work. Affordability caps the price a subscription can command, local advertising markets are too thin to backfill it, and platform after platform — Netflix and Amazon scaling back local commissioning, and the failed telco efforts before them — has learned that reach alone does not pay for content. MTN's escape from that trap is that it does not need One TV to earn its keep as a standalone streamer. It needs streaming to deepen MoMo adoption and data usage across 307 million relationships it already owns, already bills monthly, and already trusts with money. Judged as a content P&L, One TV may never look good; judged as customer-acquisition and engagement infrastructure for a US$500-billion-a-year payments business, it can be worth running even at a loss.

There is also a defensive logic that the Canal+–MultiChoice deal makes urgent. Consolidation is compressing the number of doors through which African content reaches African audiences, and a vertically integrated Canal+ will want to own billing as well as broadcast. If MTN can establish airtime-and-MoMo as the default checkout for entertainment before that happens, it does not merely sell its own subscriptions — it becomes a payment layer that even rivals may have to route through to reach the unbanked majority. The strategic prize is not One TV's subscriber count; it is being the till that every content owner, foreign or local, eventually has to plug into.
creativeMove: The genuinely original move is to treat the billing relationship as the intellectual property. Global platforms have better content, better recommendation engines and deeper pockets. What they do not have, and cannot easily build, is a two-decade-old billing rail into hundreds of millions of un-banked and under-banked wallets. When a customer pays for One TV with airtime, MTN is simultaneously the network, the merchant of record and the payment processor — collapsing into one owned stack the three separate margins Netflix must share with an ISP, a local acquirer and a card network. Every other streamer in Africa rents at least one of those layers; MTN owns all three. That is not a content advantage, it is a plumbing advantage, and plumbing is far harder to copy than a catalogue.

The scale of that plumbing is the point competitors keep underestimating. Seventy million active MoMo wallets and 23 billion transactions a year is not a fintech side-project — it is one of the largest payment networks on the continent, already handling the small, frequent, low-value transactions that streaming micro-payments require and that card infrastructure handles badly. MTN is not building a payment capability to support One TV; it is pointing an existing payment capability, built at enormous scale for remittances and merchant payments, at a new use-case. That is why the airtime/MoMo checkout is credible where a startup's 'we'll add carrier billing later' is not: for MTN the rail is the incumbent asset and the content is the experiment, exactly the reverse of everyone else's cost structure.

The music initiative sharpens the same logic from the supply side. The 'Reverberation' pitch is not 'stream more songs' — it is a promise of revenue transparency and audience data to artists who today receive precious little of either from Spotify or Apple Music. MTN Nigeria CEO Karl Toriola framed it around 'trust, transparency and equitable partnerships'; GM Funsho Finnih put it as 'the artist is our primary focus — without them, our industry diminishes.' Whether the payouts prove genuinely more equitable is unproven and should be watched sceptically. But the structural offer is real: an African-owned platform that can pay artists in local currency, straight into a MoMo wallet, with data on who is listening where, is offering creators something the global DSPs structurally cannot — settlement in the currency and the rail their audience already uses. The billing relationship is again the pitch, this time aimed at supply rather than demand.

Crucially, MTN chose to rent the part it could not own credibly. Synamedia supplies the cloud video stack — linear playout, VOD, dynamic ad-insertion, targeting — so MTN is not pretending to be a streaming-technology company, the pretence that arguably sank MTN VU's build-everything attempt in 2014. The 2026 architecture is an assembly job: someone else's proven playout technology, licensed and commissioned content on top, and underneath it all MTN's irreplaceable payment-and-billing layer. That division of labour is both more honest and more durable, because it concentrates MTN's own investment on the one layer no partner or rival can take from it. The move is not 'build a streamer'; it is 'own the toll booth and outsource the road.'
africanRead: From an African-authorship standpoint, this is the most interesting telco story on the continent — and it deserves to be graded strictly rather than celebrated reflexively. The value being captured is real and it is African-owned: the payment rail, the billing relationship, the merchant margin, and increasingly the commissioning budget for the local productions One TV carries. In a media economy where almost every layer of value flows offshore — production financing, platform ownership, the card networks that clip each transaction — an African company owning the till through which hundreds of millions of people pay for entertainment is not a small thing. Set against the Canal+ capture of MultiChoice, MTN's rail may be the single most defensible African-owned position anywhere in the continental media stack.

But owning the till is not the same as owning the culture, and the distinction is the whole of the AUTHORSHIP question. The stories, the songs, the films — the things audiences actually open the app for — are still authored by creators and, on the international slate, licensed from foreign rights-holders. The core video technology is Synamedia's, not MTN's. So MTN is building an excellent distribution-and-payment layer around cultural value it does not itself create or own. That is a legitimate and lucrative position, but it is a pipe-and-wallet position, not a studio position, and the two should not be conflated in the name of pan-African pride. The sharpest African-owned outcome would be MTN using the rail as a flywheel — recycling payment margin into originating and retaining rights in African work at scale, becoming a commissioner and owner of IP rather than only its most efficient toll-collector. The music play, with its talk of artist data and equitable splits, gestures at that ambition; One TV, as launched, still mostly aggregates other people's content.

The honest downside is not a footnote, it is central to the grade: three prior failures are signal, not noise. Reach has never been MTN's problem, and MoMo itself is the cautionary tale — a dominant network does not automatically win an adjacent market, and MoMo took years of hard operational work, not just distribution, to scale. Audiences do not stay for a payment method; they stay for the show, and across a decade MTN has never demonstrated it can pick, fund or market a hit. Owning the checkout gets a viewer to the door; it does nothing to make them want what is behind it. If the content is thin, the elegant billing rail simply processes churn more efficiently.

And there is a sovereignty paradox worth naming plainly. The same infrastructure that makes MTN the most credible African-owned route into media distribution also makes it a potential choke-point. If airtime-and-MoMo billing becomes the default way a continent pays for culture, MTN sets the take-rate and the terms for creators and viewers alike — and a rail is only benevolent until the quarter it needs to hit a margin target. African ownership of the pipe is a genuine gain over foreign ownership of it, but it is not the same as an open, contestable market for African stories. The most credible route in and a new gatekeeper are, uncomfortably, built from exactly the same wires. That tension — real African value-capture at the distribution layer, shadowed by concentration risk and an unproven ability to own the culture itself — is why this scores as a strong but strictly-bounded case, not a triumphal one.

confirmed: MTN reported 307 million customers across 16 markets at end-2025, with 172 million data customers and average monthly data usage of 12.5GB (MTN Group 2025 results).
MTN's fintech arm MoMo had ~70 million active users processing 23 billion+ transactions worth over US$500 billion in 2025 (MTN Group 2025 results).

MTN launched One TV in June 2026, built with UK video-technology firm Synamedia (partnership announced April 2025), offering free ad-supported, pay-per-view and subscription tiers (Techpoint Africa; ITEdgeNews/Innovation Village).
One TV accepts airtime deductions, MoMo wallets and, in some markets, bank cards — explicitly to remove the credit-card barrier (Legit.ng; TechAfrica News).
MTN Group's Ambition 2030 names three platforms — Connectivity, Fintech and Digital Infrastructure — and does NOT list media/entertainment as a platform (MTN Group 2025 results / Engineering News).

MTN's prior content attempts — MTN VU (South Africa, 2014–2017, closed) and Prime Video Mobile Edition (Nigeria, 2023, with Amazon, which exited Africa in 2024) — are documented; MusicTime is described as a 'modest' success (Communiqué).
reported: MTN executive Selorm Adadevoh said entertainment is 'an important gateway to digital participation' and that One TV leverages MTN's connectivity, fintech and digital capabilities (Legit.ng; TechAfrica News).

MTN Nigeria's May 2026 'Reverberation' workshop signalled a coming music platform pitched on artist revenue transparency and data, with quotes from CEO Karl Toriola and CDO A'isha Mumuni (Broadcast Media Africa).

Analysts describe African streaming unit economics as structurally unprofitable due to affordability limits and thin ad markets, with multiple telco streamers (Kwese TV, Cell C's Black, Vodacom's Video Play) having failed (Communiqué; TechAfrica News).

Canal+ completed its ~US$2bn (R35bn) takeover of MultiChoice (DStv/Showmax) in September 2025, creating an operator with 40m+ subscribers across ~70 countries and targeting €400m+ of EBITDA synergies by 2030 (The Africa Report; Variety).

Subscription payments in Africa are constrained by low card penetration and high recurring-card failure, driving reliance on direct carrier billing; Netflix already offers airtime/postpaid billing via Vodacom South Africa (Wiza Jalakasi; Retail Dive/industry reporting).
notClaimed: We do not claim One TV or the music platform is profitable, or disclose subscriber numbers or pricing — MTN has not published them.
We do not claim MTN owns or commissions the bulk of its catalogue; most content is licensed or aggregated.

We do not claim the mobile-money-as-media-rail thesis is MTN's stated strategy — it is MonoKromatik interpretation. MTN's own strategy frames content as a driver of connectivity and fintech, not a standalone platform.
We do not claim MTN will succeed; three prior content ventures underperformed or closed.

lessons.title: Own the checkout, not just the catalogue.
lessons.body: In markets defined by affordability and thin banking, the payment rail is scarcer and more defensible than content. MTN's real asset is not what plays on One TV — it is that Africans can pay for it in airtime and mobile money. Build for the wallet your customer actually holds, and you own a position no better-funded rival can replicate.

lessons.title: Rent what you can't credibly own; own what no one can rent from you.
lessons.body: MTN outsourced the streaming technology to Synamedia and concentrated its ownership on the billing and fintech layer that is uniquely its own. Vertical integration is powerful only where you hold a genuine moat; everywhere else, partnering is the honest — and faster — move.

lessons.title: Reach is table stakes, not a strategy.
lessons.body: Three hundred million relationships did not save MTN VU, and dominant reach has not made MoMo automatically win every adjacent market. Distribution gets you the shot; content quality and audience trust decide whether you convert it. Never mistake the size of your funnel for the strength of your product.

lessons.title: The most African-owned rail can become the new gatekeeper.
lessons.body: Celebrating African ownership of distribution should not blind builders to the choke-point it creates. If one company sets the take-rate for how a continent pays creators and accesses culture, sovereignty and monopoly wear the same infrastructure. Build the rail — and build the accountability that keeps it open.

pullQuotes: MTN can't out-produce Netflix. But Netflix can't bill a Lagos street vendor in airtime — and MTN can.
Streaming is the bait; the wallet is the hook. Content is not MTN's product — deeper MoMo and data usage is.

title: Sixty60: How a Grocery App Became South Africa's Most Feared Retail Weapon
standfirst: Shoprite turned its supermarkets into fulfilment centres, its startup partner into a stack it part-owns, and its loyalty data into a moat — capturing 80%+ of SA on-demand grocery while Pick n Pay bleeds.
verificationNote: Sales figures, store counts, delivery metrics and the Zulzi/Pingo structure are drawn from Shoprite's published results and reputable SA trade press. The '80%+ on-demand market share' is a Reveal Insights estimate (a Shoprite-linked research unit) — directional, not audited. Sixty60's standalone profitability is asserted by CEO Pieter Engelbrecht and not independently disclosed.

decode.label: IDEA
decode.note: Dark-store q-commerce was not invented in South Africa — but converting 875 existing supermarkets into micro-fulfilment centres, rather than burning capital on standalone warehouses, was the sharp local adaptation that made the unit economics work in a thin, price-sensitive market.

decode.label: AUTHORSHIP
decode.note: The rare case where the whole value chain stays African-owned: Shoprite (Cape Town-founded, JSE-listed) commissioned a local startup, Zulzi, to build the app — then took a 26% stake — and stood up its own last-mile carrier, Pingo, plus its own loyalty data and retail-media engine. It sells reach to suppliers instead of renting it from Uber or Instacart.

decode.label: EXECUTION
decode.note: 96.9% order fulfilment and 94.0% on-time delivery at national scale, 875 Sixty60 stores, and the fastest-growing line in SA grocery. Operationally this is best-in-class, and competitors have failed to replicate the reliability.

decode.label: CONSEQUENCE
decode.note: Sixty60 reset the competitive floor for SA grocery — Pick n Pay is closing stores and posting losses while Shoprite compounds share. The stakes are real but still national, and the gig-labour model underpinning Pingo carries its own downside.

context: In November 2019, four months before South Africa's hard COVID lockdown, Shoprite's premium Checkers chain quietly launched an app with a deceptively simple promise: fill a cart in sixty seconds, get it delivered in sixty minutes. The timing looked like luck. What happened next was not. Sixty60 did not just ride the pandemic surge in home delivery — it kept the customers after the doors reopened, and turned a defensive convenience play into the most feared growth engine in African retail. The name itself is the product spec: not a lifestyle brand, not a promise of curation, just a number that tells you exactly how fast the thing arrives. In a market where most e-commerce still means a two-to-five-day courier wait, sixty minutes was less a feature than a category reset.

The numbers are now difficult to overstate. In the six months to December 2025, Sixty60 sold R11.9 billion of groceries, liquor and general merchandise, up 34.6% year-on-year, and accounted for 10.3% of Shoprite's entire South African sales. Over the prior full year the platform moved R18.9 billion, a 47.7% jump, and by the group's own count has now fulfilled more than 100 million orders. For scale: Sixty60's turnover is now roughly 40% the size of the entire Woolworths Foods business — a food retailer built over a century — assembled inside an app in six years. According to a Reveal Insights study, it holds more than 80% of South Africa's on-demand grocery-delivery spend; an earlier read of the market by 22seven, using anonymised transaction data from over 400,000 users, already put Sixty60 at 75% in late 2021 against Pick n Pay asap!'s 13% and Woolies Dash's 12%. The lead is not new, and it has not narrowed enough to matter.

That dominance is thrown into relief by the collapse of the obvious comparison. Pick n Pay — for decades the aspirational middle-class grocer — spent 2025 closing roughly 60 company-owned stores, warning of a larger-than-expected annual loss, and watching its share price slump as its turnaround stalled. Its group revenue of R118.6 billion is now less than half of Shoprite's R252.7 billion, and where Shoprite posted a R15.0 billion trading profit up 16.6%, Pick n Pay was still absorbing a R549 million trading loss even after a painful recovery. Its delivery arm, asap!, actually grew online sales at a rate comparable to Sixty60's — but from a fraction of the base, across roughly 600 pick-up and delivery points, and never threatened the lead. The contrast is the story: two South African incumbents, the same market, the same customers — one built the last mile and the data layer itself, the other spent the decade defending a legacy estate.

It is worth naming the deeper structural point. South Africa is not an easy e-commerce market: incomes are unequal, data is expensive, and the logistics backbone that developed economies take for granted barely exists outside the metros. Those conditions have historically kept online grocery a rounding error. Sixty60's real achievement is that it made same-hour delivery work inside those constraints — profitably, its management insists — and in doing so proved that the binding constraint on African e-commerce was never consumer appetite. It was infrastructure and trust, both of which a national supermarket chain already owned.
strategicBet: Shoprite's core bet was that it did not need to build a delivery company from scratch — it needed to re-cast the asset it already had. CEO Pieter Engelbrecht has put it plainly: 'The difference between us and someone like both Takealot and Amazon is that we have this very large footprint of stores that we use as micro fulfilment centres,' rather than sinking capital into expensive single distribution centres. Every Checkers is a dark store hiding in plain sight, minutes from the customer. That is why Sixty60 could scale to 875 fulfilment points without a warehouse-building programme — and why the economics differ so sharply from the venture-funded q-commerce startups that torched billions building bespoke dark stores in Europe and collapsed. Shoprite's incremental cost per new fulfilment node is close to zero, because the node is a supermarket that was already paying rent, already stocked, already staffed. Engelbrecht insists — though Shoprite does not disclose the segment separately — that 'it is very profitable.'

The second, less-visible bet was ownership of the parts everyone else outsources. The app itself was built in roughly six months by Zulzi, a South African startup; rather than simply pay a vendor and let a critical dependency float free, Shoprite invested about R30 million for a 26% stake, binding the technology roadmap to the retailer while leaving Zulzi's founders in control. It is a deliberately unusual posture — not a full acquisition, not arm's-length procurement, but a stake large enough to align incentives and lock in the roadmap. When delivery capacity became the constraint, Shoprite made the same move at the next layer: it did not hand the last mile to a food-delivery aggregator that would own the rider relationship and the delivery data. It formed Pingo in May 2022 as a joint venture with Gauteng logistics group RTT, took 50%, and by October 2024 had regulatory clearance from the Competition Commission to absorb it outright — because, in Engelbrecht's words, 'we are growing at such a pace that it is hard to keep up with us in terms of third-party vendors' who lack the group's financial resources.

Underwriting all of it is a capital-allocation choice most of the market missed. In its 2026 financial year Shoprite funded R7.9 billion of capital expenditure out of R23.6 billion of operating cash flow, directing it at digital, data and supply-chain capability — investment made from strength, from money the business itself throws off. Pick n Pay, over the same window, had to raise roughly R12.5 billion via a rights issue and the separate listing of its Boxer discount chain, and spent much of it repairing the balance sheet rather than building forward capability. That is the quiet engine of the divergence: one retailer compounding a self-funded technology lead, the other borrowing to stay solvent. The through-line of Shoprite's bet is control at every layer — the app, the fleet, the fulfilment nodes and the customer relationship all sit inside the group, financed by the group, answerable to the group.
creativeMove: The real creative move is that Sixty60 is not, at its core, a grocery app — it is a data-capture and retail-media machine wearing an app's clothes. Every order flows through Xtra Savings, Shoprite's loyalty programme, which counts 33 million members and touches 88% of the group's merchandise sales; Pick n Pay's comparable Smart Shopper base sits around 11 million. That gives Shoprite a first-party view of what South Africa actually buys, at household granularity, refreshed daily and across income bands no single retailer has ever seen at once. Its digital unit ShopriteX then monetises that view directly, selling shopper insight and on-platform advertising back to the suppliers whose products sit on its shelves — a business that generated R647 million in marketing and media revenue in a single period, up 37% year-on-year. The delivery fee is almost beside the point; the app is a funnel into a higher-margin data and media business the competition cannot see, let alone match, and it is one of the fastest-growing profit lines in the group.

Operationally, the craft shows in the reliability numbers rather than the marketing, and the reliability is what compounds into habit. Sixty60 reports 96.9% order fulfilment and 94.0% on-time delivery at national scale — the boring metrics that decide whether a household re-orders or churns after one bruised delivery. Stress-tested at peak, the system holds: over four days of its November 2025 Early Black Friday event it delivered 7.5 million products, picked 97.6% of first-choice items in full, delivered 95.3% on time, and still landed an average grocery order in 33 minutes against a 60-minute promise, drawing more than 1.9 million app visits. The engine underneath is Pingo's fleet of more than 4,000 drivers, who supply their own bikes while Pingo covers fuel, average around 15 deliveries a day, and are paid per drop — with batched double-drops the most profitable configuration for both driver and company.

Having built the machine, Shoprite is now pointing it in every direction at once. It has extended Sixty60 down-market, launching the service under its mainstream Shoprite banner in 2025 to reach lower-income shoppers who were never the premium Checkers customer — a deliberate move to widen the funnel from the aspirational middle class into the mass market. It has extended up-stack into general merchandise, running the same rails to sell electronics, homeware and clothing, and into adjacent specialist brands such as Petshop Science and Uniq Clothing, whose combined sales grew roughly 71% by riding Sixty60's distribution and data rather than building their own. Each extension costs little and deepens the moat, because every new category is one more reason to open the app and one more stream of purchase data feeding the media business. The app stopped being a grocery channel and became the group's default interface to the customer.
africanRead: MonoKromatik's read: this is one of the cleanest examples on the continent of an African firm capturing the full stack of value in a category that global platforms usually colonise. In most markets, when a retailer goes on-demand, the last mile and the customer relationship leak to a foreign aggregator — the Ubers, Glovos and Instacarts that own the app, the rider network and, crucially, the data, leaving the grocer as a commoditised supplier of shelves who pays a commission to reach its own customers. Shoprite refused that trade at every layer. It bought into the app-maker rather than renting the software, built and then swallowed its own courier company rather than listing on someone else's marketplace, and kept the loyalty data as a proprietary asset it now re-sells to suppliers. The margin, the intelligence and the relationship that would have flowed to a platform headquartered in San Francisco or Berlin stay in Cape Town — and the technology was written by a local startup, not licensed from abroad.

That is the authorship point, and it is why Sixty60 scores where it does on our decode. The competitive moat is not the sixty-minute promise — that is copyable, and every rival has copied it. The moat is that Shoprite owns the three things that compound and cannot be bought overnight: the fulfilment footprint (hundreds of stores built over decades that double as dark stores), the delivery network (a wholly-controlled fleet, not a rented aggregator), and the data-and-media layer (33 million loyalty members feeding a retail-media business that funds the next round of investment). Each reinforces the others — more stores mean faster delivery, faster delivery means more orders, more orders mean richer data, richer data means more media revenue to fund more stores. Pick n Pay's stumble is instructive precisely because it began with the same raw assets — stores, customers, a storied brand — and did not integrate them into that flywheel with the same conviction or capital, so its e-commerce stayed a defensive cost centre while Shoprite's became a self-funding profit and intelligence engine. Ownership of the stack, not the idea, is the whole game.

We are honest about the downside, because a serious decode has to be. Growth is visibly decelerating — from 47.7% to 34.6% year-on-year — as Pick n Pay asap!, Woolies Dash, Spar2U and Uber Eats crowd the category and the easy first-mover share gets harder to defend; the celebrated 80% figure, moreover, comes from Reveal Insights, a research unit inside the Shoprite orbit, so it should be read as directional rather than audited. The Pingo model externalises capital and risk onto gig drivers who buy their own bikes and are paid per drop — a structure that looks efficient on a spreadsheet and precarious on a payslip, and one that is drawing the same labour scrutiny that has dogged delivery platforms everywhere. And the headline profitability remains management's assertion; Shoprite does not disclose Sixty60 as a reporting segment, so the market is taking the CEO's word for the unit economics. None of this dents the strategic lesson. But a network built on the virtue of owning its value chain should, in the end, be judged on whether the people carrying the last bag up the last flight of stairs share in the value they help capture — and that verdict is not yet in.

lessons.title: Own the last mile or rent your own customer.
lessons.body: The moment a retailer lets an aggregator run delivery, it loses the courier margin, the order data and the direct relationship. Shoprite bought into its app-maker and built its own fleet precisely so the customer would never belong to a platform it didn't control.

lessons.title: Your existing footprint is a fulfilment network in disguise.
lessons.body: Instead of financing warehouses, Shoprite re-cast 875 supermarkets as micro-fulfilment centres. The cheapest logistics asset is often the one already on your balance sheet — re-used, not rebuilt.

lessons.title: The app is the funnel; the data is the business.
lessons.body: Sixty60's real profit engine is a retail-media operation fed by 33 million loyalty members. Build the consumer product so it captures first-party data you can re-sell — the transaction and the intelligence are two different, stackable businesses.

lessons.title: African value-capture is a design choice, not an accident.
lessons.body: Two SA grocers had the same assets; one integrated app, fleet and data into a compounding stack and one didn't. The moat isn't the sixty-minute promise — it's who owns each link of the chain.

pullQuotes: The app, the fleet, the fulfilment nodes and the customer all sit inside the group — the margin that would have flowed to a platform in San Francisco stays in Cape Town.
Sixty60 is not a grocery app. It's a data-capture and retail-media machine wearing an app's clothes.
Pick n Pay's stumble is the lesson: it had the same stores, the same customers, the same brand — and did not own the stack with the same conviction.
